passages.title: Miles Davis
passages.text:
The career of trumpeter Miles Davis was one of the most astonishingly productive that jazz music has ever seen. Yet his genius has never received its due. The impatience and artistic restlessness that characterized his work spawned one stylistic turn after another and made Davis anathema to many critics, who deplored his abandonment first of bebop and then of “cool” acoustic jazz for ever more innovative sounds.

Having begun his career studying bebop, Davis pulled the first of many stylistic surprises when, in 1948, he became a member of an impromptu musical think tank that gathered in a New York City apartment. The work of this group not only slowed down tempos and featured ensemble playing as much as or even more than solos—in direct reaction to bebop—it also became the seedbed for the “West Coast cool” jazz style.

In what would become a characteristic zigzag, Davis didn’t follow up on these innovations himself. Instead, in the late 1950s he formed a new band that broke free from jazz’s restrictive pattern of chord changes. Soloists could determine the shapes of their melodies without referring back to the same unvarying repetition of chords. In this period, Davis attempted to join jazz phrasings, harmonies, and tonal qualities with a unified and integrated sound similar to that of a classical orchestral piece: in his recordings the rhythms, no matter how jazz-like, are always understated, and the instrumental voicings seem muted.

Davis’s recordings from the late 1960s signal that, once again, his direction was changing. On *Filles de Kilimanjaro*, Davis’s request that keyboardist Herbie Hancock play electric rather than acoustic piano caused consternation among jazz purists of the time. Other albums featured rock-style beats, heavily electronic instrumentation, a loose improvisational attack and a growing use of studio editing to create jagged soundscapes. By 1969 Davis’s typical studio procedure was to have musicians improvise from a base script of material and then to build finished pieces out of tape, like a movie director. Rock groups had pioneered the process; to jazz lovers, raised on the ideal of live improvisation, that approach was a violation of the premise that recordings should simply document the musicians’ thought processes in real time. Davis again became the target of fierce polemics by purist jazz critics, who have continued to belittle his contributions to jazz.

What probably underlies the intensity of the reactions against Davis is fear of the broadening of possibilities that he exemplified. Ironically, he was simply doing what jazz explorers have always done: reaching for something new that was his own. But because his career endured, because he didn’t die young or record only sporadically, and because he refused to dwell in whatever niche he had previously carved out, critics find it difficult to definitively rank Davis in the aesthetic hierarchy to which they cling.

summaries.standard:
**Topic**

Miles Davis's career

**Frameworks**

Theme / Example, Highlight Something Noteworthy

**Main Point**

Davis's career was incredibly productive and under-appreciated, both due in part to how many stylistic evolutions Davis went through over the years.

P1 - *Thesis*

We might have alternatively thought of this passage with a "Theme / Example" framework, since this first paragraph really lays out the overarching theme that the rest of the paragraphs unpack: *a lot of zigzags*.

P2 - *First Stylistic Zigzag*

Davis starts as bebop but then develops "cool jazz" (slower tempos and less soloing).

P3 - *Second Stylistic Zigzag*

Davis breaks free from chord patterns and seeks a more open, unified sound like that of orchestral pieces. Soloists have less constraints.

P4 - *Third Stylistic Zigzag*

Davis starts taking on more conventions of rock music -- electrified instruments and a cut-and-paste recording process that's a violation of the norms of jazz. He takes some heat from the critics.

P5 - *Author's Causal Explanation*

Here the author tries to explain why Davis was frequently maligned by contemporary critics and thus has not received his proper due as the genius he was -- critics are afraid when artists broaden possibilities or defy genre categorization (as apparently they rely on those things to do their jobs).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best states the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The Main Point correct answer usually feels like
"Topic + Purpose"

The topic was ****Miles Davis's career****.

What was the author's *Purpose* in writing about MD's career?

She wants him to get his propers. He's underappreciated because narrow-minded critics couldn't keep up with his ever-evolving style; meanwhile, continuing to chart out new, imaginative ideas is actually super on point when it comes to the central ethos of jazz music.

Do we have any Most Valuable Sentences we'll lean on in a pinch?

The first and last paragraphs are definitely where we hear the author's big takeaways on Davis's career, so some fusion of that language.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Let's look for something like
*Davis's career was incredibly productive and under-appreciated, because critics couldn't keep up with his many stylistic evolutions.*

choices.text: Because the career of Miles Davis was characterized by frequent shifts in styles, he never fulfilled his musical potential.
choices.explanation:
Our author says in the very first sentence that Davis had *one of the* *****most astonishingly productive***** careers that jazz music has ever seen.

So if ****that guy**** didn't fulfill his musical potential, then nobody does!

choices.text: Because the career of Miles Davis does not fit neatly into their preconceptions about the life and music of jazz musicians, jazz critics have not accorded him the appreciation he deserves.
choices.explanation:
The main clause is that "jazz critics have not accorded Davis the appreciate he deserves". That might sound too much like "complaining about critics" and not enough like "praising Davis", but 2/3 of the sentences in the first paragraph and 2/3 of the sentences in the last paragraph dealt with the critics, so it seems justifiable to be cool with them taking center stage in our correct answer.

The correct answer doesn't have to be perfect (and never will be); it just has to be the best available.

The final sentence of the passage matches well with
"Davis's career does not fit neatly into [critics'] ****preconceptions****"

since it says
"*[Davis] refused to dwell in whatever niche he had previously carved, so critics find it hard to rank Davis in the* *****aesthetic hierarchy***** *to which they cling."*

The second sentence of the passage says that Davis's *"genius has never received its due"*, which matches well with the idea that he has not been "accorded the appreciation he deserves".

choices.text: Because the career of Miles Davis was unusually long and productive, he never received the popular acclaim generally reserved for artists with more tragic life histories.
choices.tag: Wrong Emphasis / Out of Scope: more tragic lives
choices.explanation:
The main clause of this answer should match up with the main clause of the last sentence of the passage.

Both that sentence and this answer choice begin with the causal wind-up of ...
****Because**** Davis had an unusually long / productive career

The last sentence says that the causal result was that "****critics**** find it *difficult to rank Davis in any of their precious aesthetic hierarchies*".

This answer says that the causal result was that "Davis didn't get the ****popular**** acclaim that *people generally reserve for tragic artists*".

Those are very different meanings.

This last sentence was just saying anyone with very limited recordings (because of either dying young or not just recording much or any other reason) can more easily be pigeon-holed and understood by critics.

This answer is saying that there's a layer of praise we generally only use on artists who had a tragic life history, and we music consumers denied Davis that popular acclaim because he had a long and productive career.

choices.text: The long and productive career of Miles Davis spawned most of the major stylistic changes affecting twentieth-century jazz.
choices.explanation: The passage is exalting Davis for his many, major stylistic changes, but nowhere in the passage is there any extreme claim that says, "Davis was responsible for ****more than 50%**** of the major style changes affecting 20th century jazz".

choices.text: Miles Davis’s versatility and openness have inspired the admiration of most jazz critics.
choices.explanation: The overall gist of this passage is that critics *didn't* love Davis (because he frustrated their desire to keep people in well-defined boxes) and *didn't* sufficiently praise him, so this answer feels like the opposite of the main point.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of the "West Coast cool" jazz style?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
All our supporting text for "West Coast" cool comes from the 2nd paragraph.

We hear that this group Davis formed in an NYC apartment was the **seedbed** for the "West Coast cool" style. The seedbed is the soil and roots from which the plants grow.

So whatever Miles was doing with this group is how we would characterize "West Coast cool":

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Find a match for either/both of our available details:

- slowed down tempos
- ensemble playing was at least as common as solos (in bebop, solos took up more time than ensemble playing).

choices.text: It was popularized by Miles Davis.
choices.explanation: The New York group supplied innovations from which West Coast cool grew. The passage does not identify Davis as the person who made the style widely popular. Popularizing need not mean having the first radio hit; the missing information is about the spread of the style, not a particular distribution channel.

choices.text: It was characterized by a unified and integrated sound.
choices.explanation:
"Unified / integrated" sound doesn't match either of our available details.

- slowed down tempos
- ensemble playing was at least as common as solos (in bebop, solos took up more time than ensemble playing).

choices.text: It was played primarily by large ensembles.
choices.tag: # of members vs. Quantity of airtime
choices.explanation:
Our second detail was that "ensemble playing was at least as common as solos".

That's saying, "In a 4 minute song, at least 2 minutes of it would be dedicated to ensemble playing".

This answer is talking about the size of the ensembles: was it a 4-piece band, a 6-piece, an 8-piece?

choices.text: It introduced a wide variety of chord change patterns.
choices.explanation:
"chord change patterns" doesn't match either of our available details.

- slowed down tempos
- ensemble playing was at least as common as solos

choices.text: It grew out of innovations developed in New York City.
choices.explanation:
This answer ends up not being about the musical style itself, but we can derive this by combining claims from the 2nd paragraph.

We know that Miles's NYC band was the **seedbed** for West Coast cool, so we can support that West Coast cool grew out of what Miles did in New York City.

Was what Miles did "innovative"?

Yes, it's characterized as "the first of many surprises" / "a musical think thank" / "contrasting bebop", so we can support that it was a new thing.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests which one of the following about the kind of jazz played by Miles Davis prior to 1948?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
What do we know about the jazz Davis performed prior to 1948?

1948 is only referenced at the beginning of the 2nd paragraph. In the first sentence of that paragraph, we learn that Davis ****began his career studying bebop.****

In 1948, he joined a think tank of musicians who then decided to rebel against bebop.

But it sounds like from what we know, *prior to 1948*, Davis was playing bebop.

choices.text: It was characterized by rapid tempos and an emphasis on solo playing.
choices.explanation: The group's slower tempos and increased emphasis on ensemble playing are described as a direct reaction to bebop, which Davis had studied before1948. That contextual contrast supports faster tempos and a greater solo emphasis earlier. A reaction is not automatically the logical negation of every feature of an earlier style.

choices.text: It equally balanced ensemble and solo playing.
choices.explanation: This describes what Davis and his think tank group started doing *in* 1948, but the question was asking about what he did prior to that, which was bebop.

choices.text: It was a reaction against more restrictive jazz styles.
choices.explanation:
This describes what Davis did throughout his career, starting around 1948, but the question was asking about what he did prior to that, which was bebop.

Bebop wasn't necessarily a restrictive jazz style, but it had certain conventions that jazz critics expected. Bebop definitely is never identified in the passage as ****reacting against**** more restrictive jazz styles, and we know that Miles was playing bebop prior to 1948.

choices.text: It is regarded by purist jazz critics as the only authentic jazz style.
choices.explanation: We're looking for something that describes "bebop", but bebop was never described in the passage as something that jazz critics considered "****the only**** authentic style".

choices.text: It was played primarily in New York City jazz clubs.
choices.explanation: We're looking for something that describes "bebop", but bebop was never described in the passage as something that was "****primarily**** played in NYC jazz clubs".

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best describes the author's attitude toward Miles Davis's music?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
With *Attitude*, we initially just ask our gut, "Positive or negative?"

This author seemed very positive on Miles Davis.

1st paragraph
- **astonishingly** productive career
- his **genius** has never received its due

Throughout the passage, the *critics* have lots of issues with Davis's innovations and constant re-invention, but our author seems to love it.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for something positive that is potentially reinforcing Davis's willingness to be innovative / willingness to shapeshift.

choices.text: uneasy ambivalence
choices.explanation:
We're looking for something like "a genius with an astonishingly productive career".

This is a mild negative, and we want a strong positive.

choices.text: cautious neutrality
choices.explanation: The author calls the career astonishingly productive and Davis a genius who has not received his due. Those explicit judgments rule out neutrality here. There is no need for an unsupported claim about how often neutral has been a credited attitude in other questions.

choices.text: grudging respect
choices.explanation:
We're looking for something like "a genius with an astonishingly productive career", so the *respect* half of this answer seems fine.

But "grudging respect" means, "I kind of hate you, but I also respect you."

A lot of basketball fans didn't like Kobe but they had a grudging respect for his talents. A lot of Americans didn't like Trump but they had a grudging respect for his willingness to go against the political orthodoxy.

We don't have any support in this passage for the idea that the author didn't like Miles Davis, so we can't support *grudging*.

choices.text: moderate commendation
choices.explanation:
We're looking for something like "a genius with an astonishingly productive career".

That is a *more-than-moderate* commendation. Usually, on Attitude questions, we are expecting to pick a mild positive or a mild negative answer (and to see a strong positive or strong negative as a trap answer).

But our textual support here matches a strong positive, so in this case it's just not accurately capturing the author's admiration to say she moderately commends Davis.

choices.text: appreciative advocacy
choices.explanation:
This is the only un-tempered positive. We know the author is "appreciative". Unlike (C) and (D), this answer doesn't put some ceiling on the positivity by saying that it's a grudging respect or a moderate amount of approval.

The *advocacy* half of this is a surprise. What does it mean to say "appreciative advocacy"? It would be like our attitude towards a TV show we binged and loved.

If we're telling the world that HBO's Westworld (or BBC's Peep Show) was a genius show that for various reasons was never fully embraced by critics, we're conveying our appreciation while advocating that other people check out this show.

And in the legal sense, a legal advocate is someone providing legal counsel to you / someone defending you in court. So we can also match up the idea of 'advocacy' with the fact that the author is defending Miles against the bad rap he got with music critics.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following creative processes is most similar to Miles Davis's typical studio procedure of the late 1960s, as described in the fourth paragraph of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
For an ****Analogy**** question our Support Window consists mainly in pulling out salient adjectives, verbs, or relationships.

We know we will have to drop this topic and see the same *general* content in some other topic's clothing, so we're looking for transferrable traits or relationships.

We are told in the 4th paragraph about Davis's typical studio procedure
(*By 1969 Davis's typical studio procedure ... )*

Musicians would improvise from a base script of material, and then the finished "track" on the album would be various clips stitched together (*build finished pieces out of tape*).

It would be akin to someone writing out paragraphs of stream of consciousness for their Law School personal statement, and then extracting their favorite lines via Cut/Paste into a new document to assemble the finished essay.

So we want something that sounds like "lots of raw material, with the best parts excerpted and stitched together."

choices.text: The producer of a television comedy show suggests a setting and general topic for a comedy sketch and then lets the comedians write their own script.
choices.explanation:
This works for the first part of the process, providing the musicians with a base script of material is sort of like providing the setting / topic for a troupe of comedians and then letting them improvise the particular details.

But this doesn't have the key part that Davis did, which is go back at the end, find the best parts, and stitch them together.

choices.text: An actor digresses from the written script and improvises during a monologue in order to introduce a feeling of spontaneity to the performance.
choices.explanation:
Davis's recordings were not unedited live performances, where a musician would improvise to provide spontaneity.

He had many recordings of them improvising, and then he would combine together the best excerpts from those improvisations.

A lot of trap answers on Analogy / Parallel tasks will either repeat the same topic or repeat a similar word in order to bait us in. Here, they're trying to get us with "improvise".

This answer choice would match up better with recordings make in the classic jazz lovers style ... the musicians have a base script (the core song) to play, but then they have a passage of improvisation that lends spontaneity to the performance.

choices.text: A conductor rehearses each section of the orchestra separately before assembling them to rehearse the entire piece together.
choices.explanation:
This does sound like it captures the "combine various parts together" aspect of Davis's process. However, Davis wasn't recording the drummer, then recording the pianist, then recording the sax player.

It sounds more like he would record the whole ensemble doing Improv 1. Then he would record them doing Improv 2, 3, and 4.

Then he would pick the parts of each he wanted at assemble them together to create the final recording.

This answer has more of the feel of "separate instrumentalists are recorded, and then brought together for a group recording", but Davis's process was "do a bunch of group recording, and then stitch together the best excerpts of those group recordings".

choices.text: An artist has several photographers take pictures pertaining to a certain assigned theme and then assembles them into a pictorial collage.
choices.explanation:
*have musicians improvise from a base script of material*
matches with
*have photographers take pics pertaining to a certain assigned theme*

*assemble them into a pictorial collage*
matches with
*build finished pieces out of tape*

This answer is still somewhat different because the individual photographers are improvising by themselves, whereas the musicians were improvising together, but this is still our best available match.

choices.text: A teacher has each student in a writing class write an essay on an assigned topic and then submits the best essays to be considered for publication in a journal.
choices.explanation:
The first half of this ("here, students, improvise on this assigned topic") matches with the idea of having musicians improvise off a base script of material.

But there's no match for "build finished pieces out of tape", by combining pieces together.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's explanation for the way Miles Davis is regarded by jazz critics?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The author's explanation of critics' reaction to Davis is found in the final paragraph.

She thinks that critics were hating on Davis so much because they *feared the broadening possibilities that he exemplified. They found it difficult to definitively rank Davis in the aesthetic hierarchy to which they cling*.

Let's better comprehend that by putting it into our own words first. The critics had certain categories or genres that they use rigidly. They want people in category X to do thing Y. They want people in category X to remain there. If Davis keeps switching categories or redefining the ones he's in, it breaks down the critics' ability to use these categories. They got mad when he left the bebop category and went to cool jazz. They got mad when he left cool jazz and went towards electrified sounds.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: We can weaken the author's explanation by either proposing an *alternate* explanation for why critics didn't like Davis (alternate explanations are pretty rare in RC answers, though) or by *undermining* the plausibility of the author's story that critics love their categories and hate it when an artist switches genres or defies expectations they have about a genre.

choices.text: Many jazz musicians who specialize in improvisational playing are greatly admired by jazz critics.
choices.explanation: Since one of the expectations of the jazz genre is to improvise, it makes sense that critics would admire a jazz musician who improvises. According to the author's explanation, the critics like it when people stay within their lane and perform accordingly.

choices.text: Many jazz musicians whose careers have been characterized by several radical changes in style are greatly admired by jazz critics.
choices.explanation:
This badly undermines the author's explanation. She thought that critics were negative about Davis because he kept shifting genres, thereby defying their ability to pigeon-hole him.

This answer, though, is saying that critics had no issue with other artists who kept shifting genres throughout their career. We could call this a *Cause Without Effect* weakener, because the same supposed cause is present (radical changes in style) but the supposed effect is absent (the critics aren't being negative).

choices.text: Several jazz musicians who perform exclusively on electronic instruments are very highly regarded by jazz critics.
choices.explanation: This concerns musicians who remain exclusively electronic, not musicians repeatedly changing style. It therefore does not test the author's proposed explanation as directly as B. The passage does not guarantee that critics would admire Davis if he stayed with any one style.

choices.text: The jazz innovators who are held in the highest regard by jazz critics had brief yet brilliant careers.
choices.explanation: High regard for some innovators with brief careers is compatible with the author's suggestion that a long, continually changing career makes Davis harder to categorize. Brief careers do not inherently prevent several stylistic changes; the answer simply does not challenge the proposed explanation directly.

choices.text: Jazz critics are known to have a higher regard for musicality than for mere technical virtuosity.
choices.explanation: The author explains the critics' reaction through their difficulty with changing styles and categories, not through a musicality-versus-virtuosity standard. The proposed preference gives no direct reason to doubt that explanation. We need not claim it could weaken only one imaginable argument.

passages.title: Canon Lawyer Oversight
passages.text:
By the mid-fourteenth century, professional associations of canon lawyers (legal advocates in Christian ecclesiastical courts, which dealt with cases involving marriage, inheritance, and other issues) had appeared in most of Western Europe, and a body of professional standards had been defined for them. One might expect that the professional associations would play a prominent role in enforcing these standards of conduct, as other guilds often did, and as modern professional associations do, but that seems not to have happened. Advocates’ professional organizations showed little fervor for disciplining their erring members. Some even attempted to hobble efforts at enforcement. The Florentine guild of lawyers, for example, forbade its members to play any role in disciplinary proceedings against other guild members. In the few recorded episodes of disciplinary enforcement, the initiative for disciplinary action apparently came from a dissatisfied client, not from fellow lawyers.

At first glance, there seem to be two possible explanations for the rarity of disciplinary proceedings. Medieval canon lawyers may have generally observed the standards of professional conduct scrupulously. Alternatively, it is possible that deviations from the established standards of behavior were not uncommon, but that canonical disciplinary mechanisms were so inefficient that most delinquents escaped detection and punishment.

Two considerations make it clear that the second of these explanations is more plausible. First, the English civil law courts, whose ethical standards were similar to those of ecclesiastical courts, show many more examples of disciplinary actions against legal practitioners than do the records of church courts. This discrepancy could well indicate that the disciplinary mechanisms of the civil courts functioned more efficiently than those of the church courts. The alternative inference, namely, that ecclesiastical advocates were less prone to ethical lapses than their counterparts in the civil courts, seems inherently weak, especially since there was some overlap of personnel between the civil bar and the ecclesiastical bar.

Second, church authorities themselves complained about the failure of advocates to measure up to ethical standards and deplored the shortcomings of the disciplinary system. Thus the Council of Basel declared that canon lawyers failed to adhere to the ethical prescriptions laid down in numerous papal constitutions and directed Cardinal Cesarin to address the problem. In England, where medieval church records are extraordinarily rich, similar complaints about the failure of the disciplinary system to reform unethical practices were very common.

Such criticisms seem to have had a paradoxical result, for they apparently reinforced the professional solidarity of lawyers at the expense of the enforcement of ethical standards. Thus the profession’s critics may actually have induced advocates to organize professional associations for self-defense. The critics’ attacks may also have persuaded lawyers to assign a higher priority to defending themselves against attacks by nonprofessionals than to disciplining wayward members within their own ranks.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The failure of medieval canon lawyers' professional associations to enforce ethical standards, and possible reasons for this lack of enforcement.

**Framework**

Challenge Position

**Main Point**

Although one might expect professional associations of medieval canon lawyers to enforce ethical standards among their members, the historical evidence shows that these organizations rarely disciplined unethical behavior; this was primarily due to inefficient disciplinary mechanisms and a tendency for professional solidarity to take priority over self-regulation. ("One might expect that the professional associations would play a prominent role in enforcing these standards of conduct ... but that seems not to have happened." — end of P1.)

**P1: Expectations vs. Reality in Enforcement**

You’d think medieval canon lawyer guilds would strongly enforce ethical rules among their members, just like other guilds do and modern professional associations do, but instead they rarely got involved in discipline. Sometimes, the guilds even got in the way of discipline and discipline came from clients, not lawyers.

**P2: Possible Explanations for Lack of Discipline**

At first glance, the rarity of discipline could mean either that most lawyers were just very ethical, or that bad behavior went unpunished because the disciplinary system was ineffective.

**P3: Evidence Favors Ineffectiveness Over High Ethics**

Two points suggest the second explanation is more likely: first, secular courts, with similar standards, had much more discipline on record, which hints that church court procedures were probably just less effective, not that their lawyers were more ethical (especially since some lawyers worked in both types of courts).

**P4: Authorities Complained About the System**

Second, church leaders themselves repeatedly complained that lawyers often failed to meet ethical standards and that the disciplinary system simply wasn’t doing its job—this was a problem noted at major councils and in English records.

**P5: Criticism Backfired: Professional Solidarity**

The author suggests that criticism apparently strengthened professional solidarity. It may have encouraged organization for self-defense and a higher priority for resisting outside attacks than for disciplining members. These causal claims remain qualified, rather than established historical certainties.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best states the main conclusion of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The central topic was the curious fact that 14th century church lawyers didn't seem to be disciplined much by their professional associations.

The framework we would probably use is *Answer a Question* (aka Explain Curious Fact).

The 1st paragraph establishes the mystery:
"One might expect that X, but that seems not to have happened"

The 2nd paragraph tells us that we're hunting for the right explanation:
"At first glance, there seem to be two possible explanations for the lack of X"

The main point in an *Answer a Question* passage is whatever the author's explanation is, and the 3rd paragraph says:
"Two considerations make it clear that the second of these explanations is more plausible".

So we should make sure we understand that second consideration, and hope that there's a main point answer that sounds like that.

The first possible explanation for why "church lawyers didn't seem to be disciplined that much by their professional associations" is that church lawyers simply didn't misbehave as much. The author doesn't buy this story.

The second one is that "the disciplinary mechanisms of these professional associations were so inefficient that most delinquents escaped detection and punishment".

The final paragraph adds on the idea that most delinquent church lawyers escaped discipline from their professional associations because the associations were annoyed that outside pressures we're telling them to discipline more (like a bratty kid who chooses to do the opposite of what their parent tells them to do).

choices.text: Professional organizations of medieval canon lawyers probably only enforced ethical standards among their own members when provoked to do so by outside criticisms.
choices.explanation:
The final paragraph is saying that when these professional organizations of church lawyers got outside criticism, "it seems to have had a paradoxical result" and led to **less** enforcement of ethical standards.

The lawyers within these associations banded together to protect each other, rather than disciplining wayward members.

choices.text: Professional organizations of medieval civil lawyers seem to have maintained stricter ethical standards for their own members than did professional organizations of medieval canon lawyers.
choices.explanation:
It probably feels like the *Wrong Emphasis* as soon as we see this answer start by talking about the **civil** lawyers. They're not the central topic. The church lawyers are. We're trying to solve a mystery about why the church lawyers weren't disciplined much by their professional associations.

This answer is also contradicted because the beginning of the 3rd paragraph says that "civil law courts [had] ethical standards **similar** to those of ecclesiastical courts", whereas the answer says that civil courts had stricter standards.

choices.text: Professional organizations of medieval canon lawyers apparently served to defend their members against critics’ attacks rather than to enforce ethical standards.
choices.explanation:
The passage was trying to solve the mystery of why church lawyers were rarely disciplined by their professional associations, and its answer was that the associations were inefficient and protective of their members, so most delinquents escaped detection and punishment.

This answer certainly isn't trying to be our friend, but it's the best available answer that centers on the idea that these professional organizations were not effectively policing their wayward members.

The idea that they "apparently served to defend their members against critics' attacks" aligns with the discussion in the final paragraph.

And the idea they "didn't serve to enforce ethical standards" aligns with the idea at the end of the 2nd that "most delinquents escaped detection and punishment".

choices.text: The ethical standards maintained by professional associations of medieval canon lawyers were chiefly laid down in papal constitutions.
choices.explanation:
This answer is just pulling a detail from the passage and pretending like it's the main point. This passage was not trying to the answer the question, "what was the #1 place where professional associations of church lawyers got their ethical standards?"

If the author could only get us to take away one sentence from this passage, it would be, "the reason that church lawyers were rarely disciplined by their professional associations is that the associations were inefficient and protective of their members, so most delinquents escaped detection and punishment."

choices.text: Ethical standards for medieval canon lawyers were not laid down until professional organizations for these lawyers had been formed.
choices.tag: Wrong Emphasis: origin of ethical standards / Too Strong: not until
choices.explanation:
This answer has nothing to do with answering the central question of "how come canon lawyers weren't disciplined more by their professional organizations?"

And it makes a claim that isn't even found in the passage, that there were **no** ethical standards for canon lawyers laid down until professional organizations were formed.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which one of the following statements about law courts in medieval England is true?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
What do we hear about medieval law courts in England?

All we get is the 2nd and final sentences of the 3rd paragraph:

- their ethical standards were similar to those of church courts
- there are many more records of disciplinary actions against these lawyers than against lawyers in church courts
- some lawyers worked in both the civil courts and the church courts

Let's find an answer that reinforces one of those.

choices.text: Some English lawyers who practiced in civil courts also practiced in church courts, but others served exclusively in one court or the other.
choices.explanation:
The final sentence of the 3rd paragraph definitely says the first part of this:
*there was some overlap of personnel between the civil bar and the ecclesiastical bar*.

We know that some lawyers practiced in the civil courts and the church courts. Do we know others were exclusively civil or exclusively church?

Sure, it's very supportable / reasonable. By saying there was ****some**** overlap, the author is conveying that it was not total overlap. Also, if all the church lawyers were civil lawyers and vice versa (i.e. total overlap), then the rest of the author's conversation would make no sense.

He's considering the hypothesis of whether church lawyers on the whole were less prone to ethical failings than were civil lawyers. That question would be nonsensical if we were referring to the exact same group of lawyers. So we know some lawyers were both, but not all were both (thus some where exclusively one or the other).

choices.text: English canon lawyers were more likely to initiate disciplinary proceedings against their colleagues than were English civil lawyers.
choices.explanation: The passage reports more disciplinary actions in civil courts, but does not compare how often colleagues initiated those actions. The number of proceedings does not establish who initiated them.

choices.text: English civil lawyers maintained more stringent ethical standards than did civil lawyers in the rest of Europe.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: rest of Europe
choices.explanation: Nothing in those two sentences makes any comparison to lawyers elsewhere in Europe.

choices.text: English ecclesiastical courts had originally been modeled upon English civil courts.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: modeled on civil
choices.explanation: Nothing in those two sentences suggests that church courts were originally modeled on civil courts.

choices.text: English ecclesiastical courts kept richer and more thorough records than did English civil courts.
choices.explanation: The fourth paragraph calls English medieval church records extraordinarily rich. It does not compare their richness or thoroughness with civil records. More recorded disciplinary actions in civil courts also does not establish that those records were generally richer.

questions.prompt: The author refers to the Florentine guild of lawyers in the first paragraph most probably in order to

choices.text: introduce a theory about to be promoted
illustrate the type of action referred to in the previous sentence
underline the universality of a method discussed throughout the paragraph
point out a flaw in an argument presented earlier in the paragraph
rebut an anticipated objection to a thesis just proposed

questions.prompt: The author refers to the Council of Basel (second sentence of the fourth paragraph) primarily in order to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
This is a Local Purpose question (in order to / serves to / primarily to), so we're looking to connect this detail to the nearby Bigger Idea.

The big idea in this 4th paragraph is that there is evidence that canon lawyers definitely did misbehave.

supporting detail 1 - church authorities complained about the unethical standards of the canon lawyers and about the pathetic system for disciplining them.

supporting detail 2 - ****the Council of Basel**** declared that canon lawyers were misbehaving and ordered CC to address the problem.

supporting detail 3 - in England, there were also complaints about the failure of the disciplinary system to correct the misbehaving.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
So we want an answer choice that sounds like "the Council of Basel was mentioned as part of an illustration that ****these canon lawyers were indeed misbehaving unethically****."

The author is trying to convince us of this because she's trying to explain the lack of evidence of canon lawyers being disciplined. She's saying it could be for two reasons:

1. the canon lawyers didn't misbehave
2. the canon disciplinary system wasn't effective

And this 4th paragraph is helping to eliminate #1 as a possible explanation.

choices.text: provide an example of the type of action needed to establish professional standards for canon lawyers
choices.explanation:
The first sentence of the passage indicates that there *was* a body of professional standards defined for canon lawyers.

So it doesn't make any sense to say that the author was discussing a type of action was needed in order to establish something that was already established.

choices.text: contrast the reactions of English church authorities with the reactions of other bodies to violations of professional standards by canon lawyers
choices.explanation: The author is actually trying to present three *similar* supporting details, that all illustrate the idea that canon lawyers were indeed misbehaving, and it was just the canon lawyers had little interest in policing misbehaving among their ranks.

choices.text: bolster the argument that violations of professional standards by canon lawyers did take place
choices.explanation: The Council of Basel reported failures to follow ethical prescriptions. That is direct evidence that violations occurred, weakening the suggestion that few proceedings simply reflected scrupulous conduct. It does not establish an exact equality of misconduct rates in church and civil courts.

choices.text: explain how rules of conduct for canon lawyers were established
choices.explanation:
This paragraph is about convincing us that canon lawyers did indeed *break* the rules / did misbehave / did act unethically.

The paragraph isn't explaining how rules were established. Even the Council of Basel example makes reference to lawyers who violated "ethical prescriptions laid down in numerous papal constitutions", indicating that rules were already established.

choices.text: describe the development of a disciplinary system to enforce professional standards among canon lawyers
choices.explanation:
This paragraph is about convincing us that canon lawyers
"failed to measure up to ethical standards"
"failed to adhere to ethical prescriptions"
engaged in "unethical practices"

In all three examples, the reference to the disciplinary system is saying "it exists, but it's clearly not doing its job at policing these lawyers".

questions.prompt: According to the information in the passage, for which one of the following ethical violations would documentation of disciplinary action against a canon lawyer be most likely to exist?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The *Clue Words* in the question stem are "documentation of disciplinary action against a canon lawyer would most likely exist".

This implies that by default it's not expected that documentation would exist, but in some exceptional condition (that the correct answer will name), there *is* more hope of finding documentation.

The best *Support Window* seems to be the final sentence of the first paragraph. The rest of that paragraph had been building up the idea that guilds of church lawyers did not seem to have any interest in policing their rogue lawyers.

But, that final sentence says:
*In the* *****few recorded episodes of disciplinary enforcement******, the initiative for disciplinary action apparently came from a dissatisfied client, not from fellow lawyers.*

In other words, when lawyers misbehave, the other lawyers look the other way, so there's no documented disciplinary action.

But when lawyers misbehave, an angry client might force the issue and get a disciplinary proceeding to be conducted.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for the best match we have for our *Support Window*, something like "a dissatisfied client initiated the disciplinary action".

choices.text: betraying a client’s secrets to the opposing party
choices.explanation:
We were looking for "a dissatisfied client initiated the disciplinary action". This answer, more than any other, sounds like it could lead to a dissatisfied client who would initiate a disciplinary action.

"You told the opposition my secrets?! How dare you; you're my lawyer, you're supposed to be representing me! This can't stand. I'm going to find a way to get your guild to yell at you!"

choices.text: bribing the judge to rule in favor of a client
choices.explanation: A bribe intended to favor the client does not as directly suggest a client grievance as betrayal of the client's secrets. We should not claim every client would approve of bribery; the question asks which violation most clearly fits the documented route through a dissatisfied client.

choices.text: misrepresenting credentials in order to gain admission to the lawyers’ guild
choices.explanation: We're looking for "dissatisfied client", and this answer has nothing to do with a client.

choices.text: spreading rumors in order to discredit an opposing lawyer
choices.explanation: We're looking for "dissatisfied client", and this answer has nothing to do with a client.

choices.text: knowingly helping a client to misrepresent the truth
choices.explanation: The proposed help does not identify the direct harm to the client that betrayal of secrets does. That makes A the better fit for a client-initiated complaint. It is not a general claim that clients are necessarily satisfied when assisted in wrongdoing.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is most analogous to the "professional solidarity" referred to the first sentence of the last paragraph?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The "professional solidarity" line is saying that canon lawyers did not want to police each other's misconduct. And going even further, they would even resist outsiders' attempts to prosecute misdoing on the part of any of their members.

This might remind us of the Catholic Church's molestation scandals, in which church officials who were privy to wrongdoing committed by priests chose to cover up and protect those priests rather than take steps to hold them accountable.

(Or police departments who shield their wayward officers from being disciplined for overly aggressive conduct)

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for something where there's a group that is unwilling to go after members who misbehave and even impede the ability of outsiders to go after the members who misbehave.

choices.text: Members of a teachers’ union go on strike when they believe one of their colleagues to be falsely accused of using an inappropriate textbook.
choices.explanation:
This is an honorable form of professional solidarity. If you think your colleague is falsely accused, then you should stand up for them.

We're looking for an ignoble form --- you know your colleague is guilty, but you cover for them anyway.

choices.text: In order to protect the reputation of the press in the face of a largely hostile public, a journalist conceals distortions in a colleague’s news article.
choices.explanation:
This works. Someone within the group of journalists is trying to prevent outsiders from going after a fellow journalist for their misbehavior.

This also contains another analogous layer, "in the face of a largely hostile public". In the case of the canon lawyers, we were told at the beginning of the final paragraph that, "Such criticisms [of the canon lawyers' unethical behavior] had the paradoxical result of reinforcing professional solidarity".

When a group sees itself as "Us vs. The World", then when the world complains, the group tightens its ranks.

choices.text: Several dozen recording artists agree to participate in a concert to benefit an endangered environmental habitat.
choices.explanation:
This really has nothing to do with the same situation. The group here is "recording artists", but we don't have any mention of any recording artist who was misbehaving and other other recording artists that tried to cover up for them, rather than let them be hold accountable.

On a fuzzy surface level, we could just think, "This answer is describing nice behavior. The passage was talking about sleazy behavior."

choices.text: In order to expedite governmental approval of a drug, a government official is persuaded to look the other way when a pharmaceutical manufacturer conceals evidence that the drug may have minor side effects.
choices.explanation:
This is somewhat sketchy behavior, so we should consider it. But it's not an example of a group protecting its own members from outside scrutiny.

The government official isn't a member of the group of pharmaceutical manufacturers, so when the official covers for the manufacturer, it isn't an example "professional solidarity". They are in two separate professions.

choices.text: A popular politician agrees to campaign for another, less popular politician belonging to the same political party.
choices.explanation: There's nothing inherently sketchy about this behavior. It does represent one member of a group helping another member, but they're not covering up any misbehavior or shielding the fellow group member from outside scrutiny.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that which one of the following is most likely to have been true of medieval guilds?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
All we hear about medieval guilds comes from the middle of the 1st paragraph:

*One might expect that the professional associations would play a prominent role in enforcing these standards of conduct, **as other guilds often did**.*

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Pick the answer we can best support knowing that "medieval guilds played a prominent role in enforcing professional standards of conduct".

choices.text: Few guilds of any importance existed before the mid-fourteenth century.
choices.tag: Too Strong: few of any importance
choices.explanation:
All we know is that "medieval guilds often played a prominent role in enforcing professional standards of conduct".

We can't say anything about whether there were many important ones prior to the 14th century.

choices.text: Many medieval guilds exercised influence over the actions of their members.
choices.explanation:
All we know is that "medieval guilds often played a prominent role in enforcing professional standards of conduct".

If an organizational body plays a prominent role in enforcing standards of conduct, then do they exercise influence over the actions of their members?

Sure! The police play a prominent role in enforcing state and local laws. Do they exercise influence over the actions of the members of those states and localities? Absolutely. I don't run red lights or stop signs because of the influence of the police. I don't commit tax fraud because of the influence of the IRS.

choices.text: Most medieval guilds maintained more exacting ethical standards than did the associations of canon lawyers.
choices.tag: Contradicted, if anything / Too Strong: most
choices.explanation:
All we know is that "medieval guilds often played a prominent role in enforcing professional standards of conduct".

We can't say anything about **most** guilds. And we can't make a comparison about who had *more exacting* ethical standards.

choices.text: Medieval guilds found it difficult to enforce discipline among their members.
choices.explanation:
All we know is that "medieval guilds often played a prominent role in enforcing professional standards of conduct".

So our one support sentence sounds like the guilds found it **possible** to enforce discipline among members.

choices.text: The ethical standards of medieval guilds varied from one city to another.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: varied from one city
choices.explanation: All we know is that "medieval guilds often played a prominent role in enforcing professional standards of conduct". We can't speak to whether ethical standards varied from one city to another.

questions.prompt: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following regarding the hypothesis that medieval canon lawyers observed standards of professional conduct scrupulously?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
This whole passage is centered around the *Curious Fact* of, "How come there aren't more disciplinary proceeding against canon lawyers brought about by their professional associations?"

One possible explanation for that is that canon lawyers simply didn't misbehave that much (they behaved scrupulously, meaning 'principled behavior', rather than unscrupulously, which means 'corrupt').

We know the author rejects this potential explanation, because her main point is that the professional associations were essentially shielding their lawyers from being disciplined.

The 2nd paragraph begins by saying, "There are two possible explanations for the rarity of disciplinary proceedings: 1. canon lawyers acted scrupulously, 2. canon lawyers were commonly deviant but the disciplinary mechanisms were such that wrongdoers escaped detection and punishment."

And the 3rd paragraph begins by saying, "It's clear that the **second** of these is more plausible".

Why does the author think it's implausible that canon lawyers simply behaved better than civil lawyers?

He says that civil and ecclesiastical courts had similar ethical standards, and there are way more disciplinary actions in civil courts. And it's not like civil courts just had the "bad" lawyers, because there were lots of lawyers that worked in both the civil bar and the ecclesiastical bar.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: The author would say, "this hypothesis is undermined by certain evidence / this hypothesis is less plausible than the hypothesis that canonical disciplinary mechanisms just allowed most delinquents to escape detection and punishment."

choices.text: It is untrue because it is contradicted by documents obtained from the ecclesiastical courts
choices.explanation:
The author's position is that an alternative hypothesis is "more plausible" (1st sentence of the 3rd paragraph).

He hasn't said that this first hypothesis is **untrue** or that it's **contradicted**.

He said that it's "inherently weak", and the documentation cited in the 3rd paragraph actually comes from both civil and ecclesiastical courts.

choices.text: It is unlikely because it describes behavior markedly different from behavior observed in the same situation in modern society.
choices.explanation:
The author thinks this hypothesis is unlikely because "civil courts had many more examples of disciplining transgressors, and they had similar ethical standards and many of the same lawyers".

The author doesn't undermine this hypothesis by ever talking about the "same situation in modern society".

choices.text: It is unlikely because it describes behavior markedly different from behavior observed in a similar area of medieval society.
choices.explanation:
The author thinks this hypothesis is unlikely because "civil courts had many more examples of disciplining transgressors, and they had similar ethical standards and many of the same lawyers".

The hypothesis is that canon lawyers behaved scrupulously (behaved in accordance with honorable professional conduct).

And the author is saying, "Are we really to believe that canon lawyers behaved with rigorous integrity? That behavior would be markedly different from what we see in a similar area of medieval society, the English civil law courts. Within that area, which had many of the same lawyers, there are many examples of disciplinary actions, which suggests that lawyers in this area of medieval society were not behaving with rigorous integrity."

This answer is definitely written in a purposefully opaque way, but we can match it up better with the available supporting text better than we can any other answer.

choices.text: It is impossible to assess intelligently because of the dearth of civil and ecclesiastical documents.
choices.tag: Too Strong: impossible / Contradicted: author does assess
choices.explanation: The author definitely doesn't think it's *impossible* to intelligently assess this hypothesis, since she assesses this hypothesis, saying it's "less plausible" than an alternative explanation and "an inherently weak" inference.

choices.text: It is directly supported by documents obtained from civil and ecclesiastical courts.
choices.explanation: This answer is saying that the hypothesis is *supported* by documents, but the 3rd paragraph is saying that the documents *undermine* this hypothesis.

passages.title: Fighting Birds
passages.text:
Many birds that form flocks compete through aggressive interaction for priority of access to resources such as food and shelter. The result of repeated interactions between flock members is that each bird gains a particular social status related to its fighting ability, with priority of access to resources increasing with higher status. As the number and intensity of interactions between birds increase, however, so increase the costs to each birds in terms of energy expenditure, time, and risk of injury. Thus, birds possessing attributes that reduce the number of costly interactions in which they must be involved, without leading to a reduction in status, are at an advantage. An external signal, such as a plumage type, announcing fighting ability and thereby obviating the actual need to fight, could be one such attribute.

The zoologist Rohwer assented that plumage variations in “Harris sparrows” support the status signaling hypothesis (SSH). He reported that almost without exception birds with darker throats win conflicts with individuals having lighter plumage. He claimed that even among birds of the same age and sex the amount of dark plumage predicts relative dominance status.

However, Rohwer’s data do not support his assertions: in one of his studies darker birds won only 57 out of 75 conflicts; within another, focusing on conflicts between birds of the same age group or sex, darker birds won 63 and lost 62. There are indications that plumage probably does signal broad age-related differences in status among Harris sparrows: adults, usually dark throated, have higher status than juveniles, who are usually light throated; moreover, juveniles dyed to resemble adults are dominant over undyed juveniles. However, the Harris sparrows’ age-related plumage differences do not signal the status of *individual* birds within an age class, and thus cannot properly be included under the term “status signaling.”

The best evidence for status signaling is from the greater titmouse. Experiments show a strong correlation between the width of the black breast-plumage stripe and status as measured by success in aggressive interactions. An analysis of factors likely to be associated with breast-stripe width (sex, age, wing length, body weight) has demonstrated social status to be the only variable that correlates with stripe width when the other variables are held constant.

An ingenious experiment provided further evidence for status signaling in the greater titmouse. One of three stuffed titmouse dummies was mounted on a feeding tray. When a live bird approached, the dummy was turned by radio control to face the bird and present its breast stripe in “display.” When presented with a dummy having a narrower breast stripe than their own, birds approached closely and behaved aggressively. However, when presented with a dummy having a broader breast stripe than their own, live birds acted submissive and did not approach.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Why and how certain birds use physical signals (like plumage) to announce social status and avoid costly fights.

**Framework**

Answer / Explain

**Main Point**

The passage explores whether physical traits like plumage actually serve as honest signals of social status among birds, focusing particularly on Harris sparrows (where evidence is mixed) and the greater titmouse (where the evidence strongly supports status signaling).

The main point is captured well in the third paragraph: "plumage probably does signal broad age-related differences in status among Harris sparrows... However, the Harris sparrows’ age-related plumage differences do not signal the status of individual birds within an age class, and thus cannot properly be included under the term 'status signaling.'"

**P1: The Problem of Status and the Potential Solution**

Birds compete for resources, and those with higher social status get better access. But constant fighting is costly, so birds could benefit from external signals, like plumage, that indicate fighting ability and avoid unnecessary conflict.

**P2: Rohwer’s Status Signaling Hypothesis for Harris Sparrows**

A researcher, Rohwer, proposed that the darkness of a Harris sparrow’s throat plumage signals status—darker birds should be more dominant, even among birds of the same age and sex.

**P3: Evidence Does Not Fully Support the Harris Sparrow Hypothesis**

The actual data for Harris sparrows don’t strongly back up Rohwer’s idea. Darker birds won 57 of 75 encounters overall, but in another study of conflicts within the same age group or sex the result was nearly even: 63 darker winners to 62 lighter winners. Plumage does separate adults from juveniles, but within the same age group, it doesn’t work as a fine-tuned status signal.

**P4: Better Evidence from Greater Titmouse**

With the greater titmouse, the width of a black breast stripe is closely linked with social status, and this connection holds even when controlling for other traits like age and size.

**P5: Further Experimental Evidence with Dummies**

A controlled experiment with stuffed titmouse dummies provided further evidence: real birds acted dominant toward dummies with thinner stripes but were submissive toward those with broader stripes than their own, supporting the interpretation of plumage as a status signal.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the status signaling hypothesis holds that the ability to display a recognizable external signal would have the effect on an individual bird of

choices.text: enabling it to attract a mate of high status
allowing it to avoid costly aggressive interactions
decreasing its access to limited resources
making it less attractive to predatory species
increasing its fighting ability

questions.prompt: The author refers to the fact that adult Harris sparrows are usually dark throated (middle of the third paragraph), in order to do which one of the following?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: Paragraph 3 distinguishes broad age-related status from individual status within an age class. Adults are usually dark-throated and outrank usually light-throated juveniles; dyed juveniles also dominate undyed juveniles. These findings can support an age-related signal without establishing Rohwer's stronger claim about individual dominance. The reported study of conflicts between birds of the same age group or sex was nearly even, with darker birds winning 63 and losing 62.

choices.text: support the conclusion that plumage variation among Harris sparrows probably does not signal individual status
choices.explanation:
This connects the detail to the nearby Big Idea. This paragraph is about the author arguing "Rowher's is wrong to conclude, from his data, that dark plumage predicts dominance status".

The fact that adults tend to have darker throats than juveniles do explains why he saw a bunch of dark-throats winning, but she explains in the final sentence of this 3rd paragraph that this *age-related* dominance correlates with dark throat, but within the world of dark-throated adults, having darker throat doesn't convey higher status to that individual bird.

choices.text: argue that plumage variation among Harris sparrows helps to confirm the status signaling hypothesis
choices.explanation: The final sentence of this paragraph is the author wrapping up her counterargument by saying, "thus this ****cannot**** properly be included under the term *status signaling*."

choices.text: indicate that in light of plumage variation patterns among Harris sparrows, the status signaling hypothesis should probably be modified
choices.explanation:
The author isn't suggesting anywhere in this paragraph (or passage) that we should *modify* the status signaling hypothesis.

She's just saying that Harris sparrows are not an example of SSH, whereas the titmouse is.

choices.text: demonstrate that Harris sparrows are the most appropriate subjects for the study of status signaling among birds
choices.explanation: Since the author ends this paragraph saying that Harris sparrows ****cannot**** be properly included under the term "status signaling", she would definitely not say that they're the ****most**** appropriate subjects for studying status signaling.

choices.text: suggest that the signaling of age-related differences in status is widespread among birds that form flocks
choices.explanation: This paragraph is purely about Rohwer's interpretation of his data on Harris sparrows. There are no claims being made in this paragraph about anything that is common / rare / widespread among all birds that form flocks.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the validity of the results of the experiment discussed in the last paragraph?

choices.text: The live birds all came from different titmouse flocks.
The physical characteristics of the stuffed dummies varied in ways other than just breast-stripe width.
No live juvenile birds were included in the experiment.
The food placed in the feeding tray was not the kind of food normally eaten by titmice in the wild.
Even the live birds that acted aggressively did not actually physically attack the stuffed dummies.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best describes the organization of the passage?

choices.text: A hypothesis is introduced and studies relevant to the hypothesis are discussed and evaluated.
choices.explanation:
The first paragraph does indeed introduce the Status Signaling Hypothesis (SSH).

The 2nd paragraph discusses Rohwer's study of SSH within Harris sparrows, and in the 3rd paragraph the author evaluates this study as weak.

The 4th and 5th paragraph discuss studies of SSH within the titmouse, and the author evaluates this study as "the best evidence" for the hypothesis.

choices.text: A natural phenomenon is presented and several explanations for the phenomenon are examined in detail.
choices.explanation:
The first paragraph tells us about flocking birds that compete aggressively for access to food / shelter and status.

The passage never offers explanations for why they fight for priority of access to resources or for status.

The first paragraph also hints at a natural phenomenon of evolved traits that would signal superior fighting ability.

The passage never offers several explanations for this. The only explanation is towards the end of the 1st paragraph: "birds possessing attributes that reduce the number of costly interactions, without leading to a reduction in status, **are at an advantage**". That explains why birds might evolve a trait that would signal superior fighting ability.

This answer wouldn't touch on paragraphs 2, 3, 4, or 5, in which the passage is considering whether this status signaling hypothesis is supported by evidence.

An explanation for a phenomenon is *why* it's happening.
Evidence for a phenomenon is showing *that* it's happening.

choices.text: Behavior is described, possible underlying causes for the behavior are reported and the likelihood of each cause is assessed.
choices.explanation:
Just like (B), this is making it sound like the passage spent the whole time trying to figure why flocking birds fight and compete for resources.

We know why -- it's common sense. There aren't enough resources to go around, so living things compete for what's available.

We can't match up "plumage variations / broad breast stripe" with **behavior**, so this answer has nothing to do with status signals.

choices.text: A scientific conundrum is explained and the history of the issue is recounted.
choices.explanation:
It's hard to say the first paragraph gives us any conundrum. We speculate that birds might have evolved a signal that allows them to avoid fighting all the time to determine status.

Is that a conundrum?

And the two studies (harris sparrows and titmouse) that fill up the rest of the passage have nothing to do with telling *the history of an issue*.

choices.text: A scientific theory is outlined and opinions for and against its validity as well as experiments supporting each side are compared.
choices.explanation:
There aren't any arguments in the passage *against* the status signaling hypothesis being valid.

And there aren't any experiments trying to show it's invalid.

The study in the 2nd paragraph believes that SSH is valid and is claiming to have data that supports the validity. The author, in the 3rd paragraph, says, "That's not good supporting data. Let me show you in the 4th and 5th some better supporting data."

But nothing in the passage is trying argue that the SSH is wrong.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of Rohwer's relationship to the status signaling hypothesis (SSH)?

choices.text: Although his research was designed to test the SSH, his data proved to be more relevant to other issues.
He set out to confirm the SSH, but ended up revising it.
He set out to disprove the SSH, but ended up accepting it.
He altered the SSH by expanding it to encompass various types of signals.
He advocated the SSH, but his research data failed to confirm it.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that among birds that form flocks, a bird of high status is most likely to have which one of the following?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
If we scan or search the text for "flock" or "status", we're led to the first two sentences of the passage.

It says that birds that form flocks compete for priority access to clutch resources. Does it say anything about high status birds?

*The result of repeated interactions between flock members is that each bird gains a particular social* *****status***** *related to its fighting ability, with priority of access to resources increasing with* *****higher status******.*

From this sentence, we could derive the notion that birds with high status have better than average fighting ability, and that they have better than average access to resources such as food and shelter.

If we bring in elements of the rest of the passage, we would also probably assume that many of these high status birds possess "attributes that reduce the number of costly interactions in which they must be involved, without leading to an reduction in status".

What sort of attributes? Maybe a plumage type, such as darker throats.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Since the "attribute" stuff gets into more speculative territory, let's start by looking for an answer pulling from the two things we know more solidly about high status birds:
- they have better fighting ability
- they have better access to resources

choices.text: dark throat plumage
choices.explanation: Dark throat plumage is discussed specifically for Harris sparrows, not all flocking species. Even there, the passage distinguishes broad age-related status from individual rank within an age class. It does not deny every correlation between throat darkness and success.

choices.text: greater-than-average body weight
choices.explanation: Even though we might speculate that a high status bird won a lot of fights so probably weighs more than other birds, we don't have any text to back that up.

choices.text: offspring of high status
choices.explanation: Even though it's reasonable to think that a parent with a body type that could win a lot of fights might have offspring with a similarly winning body type, the idea that status-earning attributes are passed down is not mentioned in the passage.

choices.text: strong fighting ability
choices.explanation:
Here we finally have an answer that matches anything in the Support Window (the first two sentences).

Since "the results of repeated interactions between flock members is that each bird gains a particular social status related to its fighting ability", that suggests that a high status bird has a high level of fighting ability.

choices.text: frequent injuries
choices.explanation: The passage says fighting carries a risk of injury, but does not compare injury frequency by status. Winning does not by itself establish fewer injuries. Strong fighting ability is the directly supported trait.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following can be inferred about Harris sparrows from the passage?

choices.text: Among Harris sparrows, plumage differences signal individual status only within age groups.
Among Harris sparrows, adults have priority of access to food over juveniles.
Among Harris sparrows, juveniles with relatively dark plumage have status equal to that of adults with relatively light plumage.
Juvenile Harris sparrows engage in aggressive interaction more frequently than do adult Harris sparrows.

passages.title: Mayan Collapse
passages.text:
In *The Dynamics of Apocalypse*, John Lowe attempts to solve the mystery of the collapse of the Classic Mayan civilization. Lowe bases his study on a detailed examination of the known archaeological record. Like previous investigators, Lowe relies on dated monuments to construct a step-by-step account of the actual collapse. Using the erection of new monuments as a means to determine a site’s occupation span, Lowe assumes that once new monuments ceased to be built, a site had been abandoned. Lowe’s analysis of the evidence suggests that construction of new monuments continued to increase between A.D. 672 and 751, but that the civilization stopped expanding geographically; new construction took place almost exclusively in established settlements. The first signs of trouble followed. Monument inscriptions indicate that between 751 and 790, long-standing alliances started to break down. Evidence also indicates that between 790 and 830, the death rate in Classic Mayan cities outstripped the birthrate. After approximately 830, construction stopped throughout the area, and within a hundred years, the Classic Mayan civilization all but vanished.

Having established this chronology, Lowe sets forth a plausible explanation of the collapse that accommodates the available archaeological evidence. He theorizes that Classic Mayan civilization was brought down by the interaction of several factors, set in motion by population growth. An increase in population, particularly within the elite segment of society, necessitated ever more intense farming. Agricultural intensification exerted stress on the soil and led to a decline in productivity (the amount of food produced through each unit of labor invested). At the same time, the growth of the elite class created increasing demands for ceremonial monuments and luxuries, diverting needed labor from the fields. The theory holds that these stresses were communicated—and amplified—throughout the area as Mayan states engaged in warfare to acquire laborers and food, and refugees fled impoverished areas. The most vulnerable states thus began to break down, and each downfall triggered others, until the entire civilization collapsed.

If there is a central flaw in Lowe’s explanation, it is that the entire edifice rests on the assumption that the available evidence paints a true picture of how the collapse proceeded. However, it is difficult to know how accurately the archaeological record reflects historic activity, especially of a complex civilization such as the Mayans’, and a hypothesis can be tested only against the best available data. It is quite possible that our understanding of the collapse might be radically altered by better data. For example, Lowe’s assumption about monument construction and the occupation span of a site might well be disproved if further investigations of Classic Mayan sites established that some remained heavily settled long after the custom of carving dynastic monuments had ceased.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Why the Classic Mayan civilization collapsed and how John Lowe tries to explain it

**Framework**

Answer / Explain (with a touch of Challenge Position, as the author critiques Lowe's explanation)

**Main Point**

John Lowe uses archaeological evidence—especially the construction of monuments—to build a timeline and theory explaining the Mayan collapse as the result of multiple stresses caused by population growth, but this theory depends on possibly flawed assumptions about the archaeological record’s accuracy.

**The Most Valuable Sentence:** The third paragraph’s first sentence: “If there is a central flaw in Lowe’s explanation, it is that the entire edifice rests on the assumption that the available evidence paints a true picture of how the collapse proceeded.”

**P1: Timeline and Evidence of Mayan Collapse**

Here, we get the context for Lowe’s argument: he looks at when monuments were built to track city life. He finds that after years of growth, things fell apart (alliances broke down, death rates exceeded birthrates, and construction stopped), and within a century, the civilization basically disappeared.

**P2: Lowe’s Explanation for the Collapse**

Lowe thinks the fall was due to population growth, which stretched the land and the people too thin. Not only did farming exhaust the soil, but the growing elite class demanded monuments and luxury, pulling workers away from essential food production. All these problems spread and snowballed, especially as states fought wars for resources, causing a domino effect of collapse.

**P3: Critique and Limitations of Lowe’s Theory**

The author points out a big issue: Lowe's whole theory relies on the idea that the archaeological evidence (like monument-building) truly reflects what was happening. But what if there were still lots of people living somewhere after monument building stopped? In that case, Lowe’s timeline—and his whole explanation—could be wrong, and new evidence might change our view completely.
