questions.prompt: Which one of the following is most closely analogous to the assumption Lowe makes about the relationship between monument construction and Classic Mayan cities?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The middle of the 1st paragraph tells us about the "assumption" that Lowe makes:
*Using the erection of new monuments as a means to determine a site's occupation span, Lowe* *****assumes***** *that once new monuments ceased to be built, a site had been abandoned.*

Lowe thinks that as long as people are still at the site, they'll just keep on building monuments, apparently.

How would we go one level abstract with this, so that we can match it to an answer with a different topic?

Monuments are sort of like decorations / design improvements? So maybe the gist we're looking for is something like, "If people no longer seem to be improving / refreshing the place's appearance, then they're not actively using it anymore."

With Analogy questions, we want to always be prepared to revise what our abstract goal is, if the answer choices seem to be testing traits or relationships different from what we thought we should be focused on.

choices.text: A person assumes that the shortage of fresh produce on the shelves of a grocery store is due to the effects of poor weather conditions during the growing season.
choices.explanation:
The idea of "fresh produce on the shelves" seems most analogous to "fresh monuments at the site".

So we'd want an answer that sounds like "a person assumes that a grocery store is going out of business due to the shortage of fresh produce on the shelves".

choices.text: A person assumes that a movie theater only shows foreign films because the titles of the films shown there are not familiar to the person.
choices.explanation: This doesn't have anything to do with, "Since I don't see any more updates from thing X, I'm assuming that thing X isn't being used anymore."

choices.text: A person assumes that a restaurant is under new ownership because the restaurant’s menu has changed drastically since the last time the person ate there.
choices.explanation:
We're looking for something like "the owners have left, since there don't seem to be any new features being added".

This is more like "there are brand new owners, since there seem to be a lot of new features".

choices.text: A person assumes that a corporation has been sold because there is a new name for the corporation on the sign outside the building where the company is located.
choices.explanation:
The idea of a corporation being sold is a good match for a site being abandoned. But the part of this answer that would have to match "they've ceased building new monuments" would be "there's a new name on the sign outside".

That seems almost opposite. A better match would be like, "A corporation has been sold because they haven't run any new commercials in a while / they haven't updated their outdoor signage in a long time"

choices.text: A person assumes a friend has sold her stamp collection because the friend has stopped purchasing new stamps.
choices.explanation:
This has the same feel of, "Once new stuff has ceased, the thing has been abandoned".

Once new monuments have ceased being built, the site has been abandoned.
Once new stamps have ceased being added, the stamp collection has been abandoned.

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate

- *detailed examination of known archaeological record*

*- it is quite possible that our understanding of the collapse might be radically altered by better data*

explanationBlocks.body: Look for something like, "plausible, but could easily be disproven if we find new evidence that changes our assumptions / understanding".

choices.text: daringly innovative but flawed
choices.explanation: The idea of "daringly innovative" is pretty much contradicted by the 2nd and 3rd sentences of the passage, in which the author says that Lowe uses the ****known**** archaeological record and relies on dated monuments ****like previous investigators****.

choices.text: generally accepted but questionable
choices.explanation:
This ends up being supported by combining the early 1st paragraph with the last paragraph.

We can support "generally accepted" because Lowe uses the ****known**** archaeological record and relies on dated monuments ****like previous investigators****.

We can support "questionable" because of the final paragraph:
*If there's a central flaw, it's that the edifice rests on the assumption that the available record paints a true picture. However, it is difficult to know whether the archaeological record reflects historic activity*.

choices.text: very reliable but outdated
choices.explanation:
There's nothing in the passage suggesting that Lowe's method is *outdated* / old-fashioned, or that there is a new, modern option that's better.

Also, the author indicates in the last paragraph that relying on the archaeological is *not* very reliable. It's difficult to know whether it accurately reflects historic activity.

choices.text: unscientific but effective
choices.explanation: The author never charges that Lowe's method is unscientific in any way. After all, it makes use of the known archaeological record and relies on evidence that previous investigators also relied on.

choices.text: unconventional but brilliant
choices.explanation:
The idea of "unconventional" is pretty much contradicted by the 2nd and 3rd sentences of the passage, in which the author says that Lowe uses the ****known**** archaeological record and relies on dated monuments ****like previous investigators****.

The author also is never as effusively complimentary as "brilliant".

questions.prompt: The author of the passage would most likely agree with which one of the following statements about the use of the archaeological record to reconstruct historic activity?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The "archaeological record" appears in the beginning of the first and the last paragraphs.

However, the first paragraph has a more neutral tone that doesn't reveal the author's opinion. And the last paragraph is where we really hear from the author in this passage.

So it makes more sense that this question is directing us to what the author says about the archaeological record in the final paragraph.

There, she says
- it's hard to know how accurately the archaeological record reflects historic activity, especially given the complexity of the group being studied
- it's quite possible that if we had better data (new evidence added to the archaeological record), that it would radically alter our understanding of the Mayan collapse.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for a safely worded, supportable answer, probably deriving its support from one of those two sentiments we dug out of the last paragraph.

choices.text: With careful analysis, archaeological evidence can be used to reconstruct accurately the historic activity of a past civilization.
choices.explanation: This sounds way too optimistic about the ability of the archaeological record to give us an ****accurate**** version of history. The author's comments in the last paragraph reflect much more uncertainty: "We don't know how reliable this record is. New information we might discover could easily unravel our theories."

choices.text: Archaeological evidence is more useful for reconstructing the day-to-day activities of a culture than its long-term trends.
choices.explanation:
The only comparison the author seems to make in the last paragraph comes from the "especially". We could probably say she'd agree that the archaeological record provides a more uncertain picture for complex civilizations than for simpler ones.

But we don't have ammunition to support any contrast between day-to-day and long-term trends.

choices.text: The accuracy of the archaeological record for reconstructing historic activity is dependent on the duration of the particular civilization.
choices.explanation:
Nothing in the last paragraph speaks to a causal relationship between "accuracy" and "duration".

The only causal difference-maker alluded to is a relationship between "accuracy" and "complexity".

choices.text: The archaeological record is not an appropriate source of data for reconstructing historic activity.
choices.explanation:
This is the flipside of (A). Now we're going too much in a pessimistic direction. The author isn't saying we ****shouldn't**** use the archaeological record.

She's just sprinkling in some reminders that our understanding of the Mayan collapse is inherently uncertain, given the limitations of the archaeological record.

choices.text: Historic activity can be reconstructed from archaeological evidence, but it is ultimately impossible to confirm the accuracy of the reconstruction.
choices.explanation: The author says reconstructions can be tested only against the best available evidence, whose accuracy as a picture of past activity is itself uncertain. New data could overturn the chronology. This supports the lack of definitive confirmation independent of that record, while allowing evidence-based reconstruction. It does not follow merely from being falsifiable that a hypothesis can never receive confirmation, and this choice should not become a universal rule against historical knowledge.

passages.title: Jury Impartiality
passages.text:
The expansion of mass media has led to an explosion in news coverage of criminal activities to the point where it has become virtually impossible to find citizens who are unaware of the details of crimes committed in their communities. Since it is generally believed that people who know the facts of a case are more likely than those who do not to hold an opinion about the case, and that it is more desirable to empanel jurors who do not need to set aside personal prejudices in order to render a verdict, empaneling impartial juries has proven to be a daunting task in North American courts, particularly in trials involving issues or people of public interest.

Judges rely on several techniques to minimize partiality in the courtroom, including moving trials to new venues and giving specific instructions to juries. While many judges are convinced that these techniques work, many critics have concluded that they are ineffective. Change of venue, the critics argue, cannot shield potential jurors from pretrial publicity in widely reported cases. Nor, they claim, can judges’ instructions to juries to ignore information learned outside the courtroom be relied upon; one critic characterizes such instruction as requiring of jurors “mental contortions which are beyond anyone’s power to execute.”

The remedy for partiality most favored by judges is *voir dire*, the questioning of potential jurors to determine whether they can be impartial. But critics charge that this method, too, is unreliable for a number of reasons. Some potential jurors, they argue, do not speak out during *voir dire* (French for “to speak the truth”) because they are afraid to admit their prejudices, while others confess untruthfully to having prejudices as a way of avoiding jury duty. Moreover, some potential jurors underestimate their own knowledge, claiming ignorance of a case when they have read about it in newspapers or discussed it with friends. Finally, the critics argue, judges sometimes phrase questions in ways that indicate a desired response, and potential jurors simply answer accordingly.

These criticisms have been taken seriously enough by some countries that rely on juries, such as Canada and Great Britain, that they have abandoned *voir dire* except in unusual circumstances. But merely eliminating existing judicial remedies like *voir dire* does not really provide a solution to the problem of impartiality. It merely recognizes that the mass media have made total ignorance of criminal cases among jurors a virtual impossibility. But if a jury is to be truly impartial, it must be composed of informed citizens representative of the community’s collective experience; today, this experience includes exposure to mass media. Impartiality does not reside in the mind of any one juror, it instead results from a process of deliberation among the many members of a panel of informed, curious, and even opinionated people.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The challenges of ensuring impartial juries in the age of mass media coverage of crime.

**Framework**

Problem / Solution

**Main Point**

Because mass media makes it nearly impossible for jurors to be totally ignorant of criminal cases, traditional methods for ensuring impartiality—like voir dire, change of venue, and judge’s instructions—are often ineffective; true impartiality comes from the collective deliberation of a diverse and informed jury, not from isolating each individual juror from information and opinion. **The Most Valuable Sentence appears in the last paragraph: "But if a jury is to be truly impartial, it must be composed of informed citizens representative of the community’s collective experience; today, this experience includes exposure to mass media."**

**P1: The Complication of Empaneling Impartial Juries in the Media Age**

The huge increase in crime coverage by mass media means everyone knows details about criminal cases, making it really hard to find jurors who can be unbiased or truly impartial, especially in high-profile cases.

**P2: Traditional Judicial Remedies and Their Critics**

Judges use strategies like moving trials or giving strict instructions to the jury to reduce bias, but critics say these don’t actually work—people can’t really ignore what they already know, especially for well-publicized cases.

**P3: Problems with Voir Dire (Jury Questioning)**

The main method judges rely on is questioning jurors during jury selection to weed out bias, but critics point out a lot of flaws: some people hide their true feelings, some lie to avoid serving, some underestimate what they know, and sometimes judges unintentionally lead people to a desired answer.

**P4: Rethinking Impartiality in Jury Selection**

Some countries have given up on voir dire, but that doesn’t solve the problem—instead, it just admits that keeping jurors completely uninformed is impossible today. The real solution is to embrace that juries will be informed and to recognize that impartiality is achieved through group discussion and collective experience, not individual ignorance.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Due to the expansion of mass media, traditional methods for ensuring the impartiality of jurors are flawed and must be eliminated so that other methods can be implemented.
Criticisms of traditional methods for ensuring the impartiality of jurors have led some countries to abandon these methods entirely.
Of the three traditional methods for ensuring the impartiality of jurors, voir dire is the most popular among judges but is also the most flawed.
Voir dire is ineffective at ensuring impartiality due to the latitude it offers potential jurors to misrepresent their knowledge of the cases they are called to hear.
Due to the expansion of mass media, solving the problem of minimizing partiality in the courtroom requires a redefinition of what constitutes an impartial jury.

questions.prompt: One critic characterizes judges' instructions as requiring "mental contortions" (end of the second paragraph) most likely because of a belief that jurors cannot be expected to

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The important support text on most *Meaning in Context* questions comes from the sentence or two leading-up to the word/phrase.

Right before we hear the 'mental contortions' line, we hear critics say that "we can't rely upon judges' instruction to juries to ignore information learned outside the courtroom".

So apparently judges tell juries, "You're only allowed to use what you hear in this courtroom, in making your decision. Ignore any information you've learned outside the courtroom."

And the critics doubt that this will work. They think it's asking jurors to do something incredibly unnatural (contortions) that is beyond their power to execute.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: So the critics think that jurors cannot be expected to **ignore information learned outside the courtroom when thinking/deliberating about a case**.

choices.text: deliberate only on what they learn in a trial and not on what they knew beforehand
choices.explanation:
This seems like the best available match for what we're looking for:

**ignore information learned outside the courtroom when thinking/deliberating about a case**.

"Outside the courtroom" is the same here as "what they knew beforehand". They should ignore stuff they've learned outside the courtroom and deliberate only on what they learn in a trial.

choices.text: distinguish between pretrial speculation and the actual facts of a case
choices.explanation:
This might be temptingly similar to what we're looking for:

**ignore information learned outside the courtroom when thinking/deliberating about a case**.

We might think of "outside the courtroom" as being a decent match for "pretrial speculation". We might think of "inside the courtroom" being the actual facts of a case.

In that case, "mental contortions" refers to the critics' belief that jurors cannot be expected to **ignore** pretrial speculation and attend only to the actual facts of the case.

There are two issues there
1. "Being able to distinguish between stuff we learned from X and stuff we learned from Y" is not the same thing as "ignoring stuff we learned from X and thinking only about what we learned from Y".

In order to ignore X, you'd have to distinguish X from Y, but critics aren't skeptical that we can distinguish the two. They're skeptical that we can ignore X.

2. this answer is referring to the "outside courtroom" stuff as "pretrial **speculation**", whereas the passage was talking about "learning **information**" outside the courtroom.

It wasn't saying that what jurors were getting out of the courtroom was rumor or innuendo or speculation. They were just saying it was inadmissible to the trial, if it wasn't actually presented during the trial.

choices.text: hear about a case before trial without forming an opinion about it
choices.explanation:
This does not match what we're looking for:

**when thinking / deliberating about a case, ignore information learned outside the courtroom**

"ignoring information" is not the same thing as "not-forming an opinion".

This answer also refers to the pre-trial phase, whereas the mental contortions referred to the actual trial phase.

choices.text: identify accurately the degree of prior knowledge they may possess about a case
choices.explanation:
This does not match what we're looking for:

**when thinking / deliberating about a case, ignore information learned outside the courtroom**

"accurately self-assessing your prior knowledge" is not the same thing as "ignore / suppress information learned outside the courtroom".

choices.text: protect themselves from widely disseminated pretrial publicity
choices.explanation:
This does not match what we're looking for:

**when thinking / deliberating about a case, ignore information learned outside the courtroom**

"avoiding widespread pretrial publicity" does not mean the same thing as same thing as "ignore / suppress information learned outside the courtroom".

If some one avoids widespread publicity, they'll remove one source of information they could learn outside the courtroom. But they could still learn about the case from speaking to people familiar with it or by exposing themselves to moderately disseminated pretrial publicity.

The critics are saying that people will have a hard time ignoring the totality of stuff they've learned outside the courtroom (potentially from a myriad of sources).

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the third paragraph is to

choices.text: propose a new method of ensuring impartiality
describe criticisms of one traditional method of ensuring impartiality
argue against several traditional methods of ensuring impartiality
explain why judges are wary of certain methods of ensuring impartiality
criticize the views of those who believe judges to be incapable of ensuring impartiality

questions.prompt: With which one of the following statements would the author be most likely to agree?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Since this question stem has a totally *Undefined Target*, we can head straight to the answers or remind ourselves of the author's main point(s), even though the question isn't necessarily going to test us on that.

The author's main point / voice was actually very contained in the final paragraph. The rest of the passage involves a pretty neutral presentation of ideas. So because of that, we have a *Semi-Defined Target* -- we can pretty safely assume the correct answer will be dealing with the last few sentences, starting from that first "But".

- getting rid of *voir dire* doesn't solve the problem of impartiality

- instead of looking for "blank slates", think of impartiality as what results when you get a bunch of informed / curious / even-opinionated people together.

choices.text: Flaws in *voir dire* procedures make it unlikely that juries capable of rendering impartial decisions can be selected.
choices.explanation:
The author's last few sentences are saying that you can have an impartial jury that is composed of people who have had prior exposure to the subject matter in a trial via mass media exposure.

Impartiality ≠ a juror who is oblivious to the case
Impartiality = a process of deliberation among the members of the jury (even if they already have an opinion on the case when they show up)

So since the author thinks impartiality is very achievable, as long as we redefine it, she wouldn't say "it's unlikely that juries capable of impartiality can be selected".

choices.text: Knowledge of a case before it goes to trial offers individual jurors the best chance of rendering impartial decisions.
choices.explanation:
The author is saying that we can be *tolerant* of jury members' having prior exposure to some of a case's details, via mass media exposure.

If that exposure is representative of the community's collective experience, then we're good.

But the author isn't saying that prior knowledge is a *necessary* ingredient to achieving the **best** kind of impartial decisions. If there were a case that didn't have any mass media exposure, then it would be more representative of the community's collective experience to not have any prior knowledge.

The author isn't suggesting that in such circumstances, the best jury members would be the weirdos who for some reason had prior knowledge of the case.

choices.text: Jurors who bring prior opinions about a case to their deliberations need not decrease the chance of the jury’s rendering an impartial decision.
choices.explanation:
This has the very weak language we're attracted to:
*People who are X need not do Y*
just means that "in at least one case, someone could be X but not Y".

Does this author think that it's possible sometimes for jurors to bring prior opinions about a case, but it **doesn't** decrease the chance of an impartial decision?

Certainly! Her idea at the end is that impartiality isn't dependent on whether the minds of individual jurors have prior opinions. It's dependent on a process of deliberation among the many members of the panel. So the jury can still render an impartial decision *even if* the people empaneled are opinionated when it comes to this case.

choices.text: Only juries consisting of people who bring no prior knowledge of a case to their deliberations are capable of rendering truly impartial decisions.
choices.explanation:
The author's main point is basically the opposite of this. This represents the old conception of impartiality (individual jurors have no prior knowledge).

The author is re-defining impartiality as something that results from the process of deliberation among jury members, some/all of whom may have prior opinions.

choices.text: People who know the facts of a case are more opinionated about it than those who do not.
choices.explanation: The opening reports a general belief that knowing the facts makes someone more likely to hold an opinion. That differs from having a stronger degree of opinionatedness, and it is not presented as the author's own conclusion. The author's final argument instead concerns collective deliberation. No outside political or medical example is needed.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that a potential benefit of mass-media coverage on court cases is that it will

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body: The final paragraph says a truly impartial jury should represent the community's collective experience, which today includes mass-media exposure. It then locates impartiality in deliberation among informed, curious and even opinionated members. The possible benefit is to that collective process, not a guarantee that exposure makes each individual less biased.

choices.text: determine which facts are appropriate for juries to hear
choices.explanation:
Nothing in our available sentences is talking about which facts are *appropriate* for juries to hear.

And how on Earth would *mass media exposure* determine which facts are appropriate? Does that mean that the lawyers would think, "It's inappropriate to repeat any facts during this trial that juries would have already heard about through mass media exposure"?

That doesn't sound like anything we read.

choices.text: improve the ability of jurors to minimize their biases
choices.explanation:
This is somewhat tempting, because the passage is saying that mass media exposure could improve the ability of ****juries**** to achieve ****impartiality**** (as the author is redefining it).

But the author is never saying that an individual juror, by being exposed to mass media, is better able to be unbiased (impartial) on a personal level.

She thinks that these exposed jurors will be *opinionated* people, which doesn't quite mean *biased* in the harshest sense of the word, but it does mean they are not blank slates.

choices.text: strengthen the process by which juries come to decisions
choices.explanation:
We were looking for something like, "the benefit of exposure is that it helps a jury with its goal of impartiality".

Impartiality (as the author defines it) = composed of citizens representative of the community's collective experience, which includes exposure to mass media.

This answer choice is taking our prediction, "Helps a jury with its goal of impartiality" and swapping out "its goal of impartiality" with the way that goal is described in the final sentence of the passage:

*impartiality results from a process of deliberation among members of a panel of* *****informed******, curious, and even* *****opinionated***** *people.*

If mass exposure leads to people being more informed and opinionated, and the process of deliberation (how juries come to decisions) is meant to include a panel of informed/opinionated people, then we can say that mass exposure helps with the process by which juries deliberate a case.

Tough answer, though. Definitely a "best available" last resort.

choices.text: change the methods judges use to question potential jurors
choices.tag: Out of Scope: methods of questioning
choices.explanation: Nothing in these final sentences is saying that one benefit of mass exposure is that it's changing the methods that judges use when questioning potential jurors.

choices.text: increase potential jurors’ awareness of their degree of bias
choices.tag: Out of Scope: awareness of bias
choices.explanation: Nothing says mass-media exposure makes individual jurors more aware of their biases. The author distinguishes collective deliberation from an individual juror's state of mind. Opinionated does not mean necessarily biased, and an impartial jury is not defined merely as any group of average people.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following principles is most in keeping with the passage's argument?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Since they're asking for a principle that's in line with the passage's **argument** we should think about the author's Conclusion (main point) as well as the author's Evidence (supporting reasons).

The author's main point is that we should re-think our definition of "impartiality". It doesn't have to mean "oblivious to any details of a case". It could instead mean, "the result of a group of representative citizens deliberating over a case".

Why is the author selling us on this idea?

She's saying that it's nearly impossible to find oblivious jurors for high profile cases, and that the process of *voir dire* is not super successful at actually ending up with oblivious jurors.

Getting rid of *voir dire* wouldn't solve the problem, but redefining how we think about impartiality could.

Let's primarily look for an answer that aligns with our author's stance on this issue.

choices.text: Jurors should put aside their personal experiences when deliberating a case and base their decision only on the available information.
choices.explanation:
The author never says that jurors should put aside their personal experiences.

She thinks that impartiality results from a process of deliberation among the "many members of a panel of informed, curious, and even opinionated people".

The notion of being informed and opinionated goes hand in hand with drawing upon personal experience from outside the courtroom.

choices.text: Jurors should rely on their overall experience when deliberating a case even when the case was subject to mass-media exposure before trial.
choices.explanation:
This is the flip of (C), and this one aligns with the author's stance in the final paragraph.

*If a jury is to be truly impartial, it must be composed of informed citizens representative of the community's collective experience; **today, this experience includes exposure to mass media***

The author thinks it's okay for jurors to be opinionated people who have heard pretrial stuff about the case; this is what makes them representative of the community's collective experience, and impartiality results from the process of such people deliberating together.

choices.text: Jurors should make every effort when deliberating a case to ignore information about the case that they may have learned from the mass media.
choices.explanation:
The author is NOT part of the crowd of people who are determined to find oblivious jurors or to force jurors to ignore information learned outside the classroom, which is described as "mental contortions which are beyond anyone's power to execute".

The author is okay with jurors being opinionated people. She thinks that impartiality isn't found in the mind of each juror but rather in the process of representative citizens collaborating and deliberating on a verdict.

choices.text: Jurors should be selected to hear a case based on their degree of exposure to mass-media coverage of the case before trial.
choices.tag: Too Strong: based on their degree
choices.explanation:
The author would not say, "We should pick jurors based on who has the least exposure to mass-media coverage before the trial".

After all, she says this about impartial juries:

*If a jury is to be truly impartial, it must be composed of informed citizens representative of the community's collective experience; **today, this experience includes exposure to mass media***

But she also wouldn't say that "We should pick jurors based on who has the MOST exposure to mass-media coverage".

She isn't saying that mass-media exposure is the way we decide who makes the jury. She's just saying that mass-media exposure shouldn't be a dealbreaker that keeps somebody off a jury.

choices.text: Jurors should be selected to hear a case based on their capacity to refrain from reading or viewing mass-media coverage of the case while the trial is in progress.
choices.tag: Too Strong: based on capacity to refrain
choices.explanation:
This again sounds like the people who worry about jurors being blank slates with no previous knowledge of a trial.

The author isn't part of that crowd. She's cool with jurors having exposure to mass-media coverage prior to the trial.

This answer, though, is talking about whether jurors should be gaining even more mass-media exposure to the trial while it's in progress.

Our author never expresses any specific view about mass-media exposure during the trial, but we have no basis for supporting this strongly worded answer that, "Jurors should be selected **based on this criterion**: how capable they are of refraining from being exposed to mass-media coverage of the case while the trial is in progress".

questions.prompt: Of the following, the author's primary purpose in writing the passage most likely is to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Normally for Primary Purpose questions, we lean on our Framework.

For this passage we probably used a *Problem / Solution* framework, since the first sentence starts out by saying “X has led to Y to the point where it is ****virtually impossible**** to find citizens who are unaware of the details of local crimes” and the end of the first paragraph is saying, “Empaneling impartial juries has proven to be a **daunting** task."

Once the author establishes the Problem, the 2nd paragraph discusses several potential Solutions judges use, techniques meant to minimize partiality. The author makes it seem like these are unsatisfactory solutions.

Then the 3rd paragraph discusses *voir dire*, the most favored Solution, but the author also makes it seem like this is an unsatisfactory answer.

In the final paragraph, the author's voice comes blazing through.
*Merely eliminating existing remedies like voir dire does not really provide a solution ...*

And then the author proposes her Solution: we rethink what we mean by impartiality. Instead of thinking of it as residing in the mind of a juror who has no prior knowledge or opinions of a case, we can think of it as the result of opinionated, informed people deliberating.

So let's look for something like "propose a solution to a problem".

choices.text: search for compromise between proponents and critics of *voir dire*
choices.explanation:
*Voir dire* was just one of several potential solutions that the author presents but then undermines.

The author's main agenda in writing this passage was to make the proposed solution she offers in the final two sentences of the passage, not to find a compromise between lovers and haters of *voir dire*.

choices.text: call attention to the effects of mass media on court proceedings
choices.explanation:
This answer makes it sound like the author wrote this passage just to publicize the Problem discussed in the 1st paragraph.

But since the author ends with a Solution / Recommendation, then we have to consider *that* the primary reason why she wrote the passage. If she could only leave us with one sentence, it would be her solution/recommendation (found in the last couple sentences).

choices.text: encourage judges to find new ways to ensure impartial jurors
choices.explanation:
The author's solution doesn't have anything to do with judges doing new things. And it's very harsh to say that anything would ever **ensure** impartial jurors.

The author's solution is more or less to stop considering the Problem a problem. She's saying, "Don't worry about the fact that many jurors will have some previous knowledge and even a previous opinion about a case. Trust that impartiality comes through the process of deliberation, not by each juror being a blank slate."

choices.text: debate critics who find fault with current *voir dire* procedures
choices.explanation:
*Voir dire* was just one of several potential solutions that the author presents but then undermines.

The author's main agenda in writing this passage was to make the proposed Solution she offers in the final two sentences of the passage, not to debate critics how don't like *voir dire*.

At no point is the author ever **defending** *voir dire.* She even seems to recognize the merit of the criticisms because she's saying, "some countries agree with these criticisms so much that they've abandoned using *voir dire."*

The author is here to present a Solution, which this answer fails to capture.

choices.text: argue for a change in how courts address the problem of impartiality
choices.explanation:
This sounds the most like "propose a Solution to the Problem of impartiality".

The author has considered other people's attempts at solving the problem and then immediately presented ideas that undermine those solutions.

In the end, she says that eliminating *voir dire* doesn't solve the impartiality problem. It just recognizes that *voir dire* ain't the solution.

The solution, she says in the final two sentences, is to just redefine what we think "impartiality" means. Instead of trying to find jurors that are oblivious to the case they're going to be assigned to, courts can just think of an impartial jury as one that seems representative of the community's collective experience.

If most people in the local community have already heard about the case and formed some opinions, then it's fine if most of the jurors have those characteristics too. That's because impartiality isn't about having jurors who were a blank slate; it's the result of a process of deliberation between people.

passages.title: Hopi Personal Names
passages.text:
Personal names are generally regarded by European thinkers in two major ways, both of which deny that names have any significant semantic content. In philosophy and linguistics, John Stuart Mill’s formulation that “proper names are meaningless marks set upon persons to distinguish them from one another” retains currency; in anthropology, Claude Lévi-Strauss’s characterization of names as being primarily instruments of social classification has been very influential. Consequently, interpretation of personal names in societies where names have other functions and meanings has been neglected. Among the Hopi of the southwestern United States, names often refer to historical or ritual events in order both to place individuals within society and to confer an identity upon them. Furthermore, the images used to evoke these events suggest that Hopi names can be seen as a type of poetic composition.

Throughout life, Hopis receive several names in a sequence of ritual initiations. Birth, entry into one of the ritual societies during childhood, and puberty are among the name-giving occasions. Names are conferred by an adult member of a clan other than the child’s clan, and names refer to that name giver’s clan, sometimes combining characteristics of the clan’s totem animal with the child’s characteristics. Thus, a name might translate to something as simple as “little rabbit,” which reflects both the child’s size and the representative animal.

More often, though, the name giver has in mind a specific event that is not apparent in a name’s literal translation. One Lizard clan member from the village of Oraibi is named Lomayayva, “beautifully ascended.” This translation, however, tells nothing about either the event referred to—who or what ascended—or the name giver’s clan. The name giver in this case is from Badger clan. Badger clan is responsible for an annual ceremony featuring a procession in which masked representations of spirits climb the mesa on which Oraibi sits. Combining the name giver’s clan association with the receiver’s home village, “beautifully ascended” refers to the splendid colors and movements of the procession up the mesa. The condensed image this name evokes—a typical feature of Hopi personal names—displays the same quality of Western Apache place names that led one commentator to call them “tiny imagist poems.”

Hopi personal names do several things simultaneously. They indicate social relationships—but only indirectly—and they individuate persons. Equally important, though, is their poetic quality; in a sense they can be understood as oral texts that produce aesthetic delight. This view of Hopi names is thus opposed not only to Mill’s claim that personal names are without inherent meaning but also to Lévi-Strauss’s purely functional characterization. Interpreters must understand Hopi clan structures and linguistic practices in order to discern the beauty and significance of Hopi names.

summaries.standard:
**Central Topic / Purpose**

*significance of Hopi Names* / *Clarify Misconception*
*(*or *Highlight Something Overlooked)*

**Main Point**

Unlike Mill's point of view (that names are meaningless) or Strauss's (that names are primarily instruments of social classification), the correct view of Hopi names is that they were extremely meaningful things that not only helped to indicate social relationships but also provided aesthetic delight because of their poetic beauty or significance.

**Passage Map**

*P1 - Introduce other views on function of names before pivoting into Passage's focus: Hopi Names.*

*P2 - Background information on when and how Hopis receive names*

*P3 - Elaboration on naming process, illuminated by an example, culminating in a takeway that the names are like tiny poems*

*P4 - Author's summary of Hopi names, showing how neither of the views on function in names from P1 are adequate in describing Hopi names.*

**Other Commentary**

In trying to solve the passage from the 1st paragraph, there are a few foreshadowing hints:
1st sentence: "Personal names are ****generally**** regarded in two ways ..."

The fact that there are two views on how to regard personal names would prompt us to think, "Maybe we should organize this passage with a ****Present a Debate**** framework****".****

The wording that "X is ****generally**** thought of as Y" foreshadows a ****Clarify a Misconception / Highlight Something Overlooked**** type passage.

When we see the 3rd sentence say, "Consequently, X has been neglected", we would think, "Okay, the author's primary focus in this passage is to look at societies where names have *other* functions and meanings".

In this sense, we could see the passage as a ****Illustrate by Example****, in which the discussion of Hopi names is just the example used to illustrate the broader point that some societies use names for functions that go beyond what our two guys enumerated in the 2nd sentence.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements most accurately summarizes the passage's main point?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body: The last sentence of the 1st paragraph is a decent proxy for Main Point, although the author's voice really came through in the final paragraph.

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipating Answer
explanationBlocks.body: It should emphasize that Hopi names *do* have semantic content (i.e. "meaning) / poetic properties, unlike the conception of names that Mill / Strauss and other European thinkers have.

choices.text: Unlike European names, which are used exclusively for identification or exclusively for social classification, Hopi names perform both these functions simultaneously.
choices.explanation:
The author isn't saying in the end, "It's not what Mill is saying; it's not what Strauss is saying. It's *both*."

The author is saying in the end, "Hopi names are definitely not what Mill is saying, and they do *more* than what Strauss is saying."

This answer leaves out the main idea, that Hopi names *do* have semantic content and poetic properties (meaning, and even beauty).

choices.text: Unlike European names, Hopi names tend to neglect the functions of identification and social classification in favor of a concentration on compression and poetic effects.
choices.explanation:
Again we would want to compare this language to that in the final paragraph. The author isn't saying that Hopi names *do not* identify or socially classify.

She says that "Hopi names do several things simultaneously" and two of those are indirectly indicate social relationships and directly individuate persons.

choices.text: Lacking knowledge of the intricacies of Hopi linguistic and tribal structures, European thinkers have so far been unable to discern the deeper significance of Hopi names.
choices.explanation: The passage criticizes narrow characterizations and explains Hopi names' meaningful and aesthetic functions. It does not establish the specific causal explanation that European thinkers lack knowledge of tribal and linguistic structures. A main-point answer need not use a particular grammatical subject; this answer lacks the passage's actual central claim.

choices.text: Although some Hopi names may seem difficult to interpret, they all conform to a formula whereby a reference to the name giver’s clan is combined with a reference to the person named.
choices.explanation:
If the author could only leave us with one idea, would it be that "*all* Hopi names conform to the same formula"? Probably not.

She framed this discuss not as a how-to-make a Hopi name conversation, but rather a "What is the significance of a name?" conversation.

The main point needs to address that main theme. Nothing in this answer choice reinforces the Purpose of going against the typical sense of a name having no semantic content and existing only to identify or socially classify.

choices.text: While performing the functions ascribed to names by European thinkers, Hopi names also possess a significant aesthetic quality that these thinkers have not adequately recognized.
choices.explanation:
This reinforces the "Hopi names perform several functions at once" framing idea of the last paragraph. They do identify (as Mills thought) and socially classify (as Strauss thought), but *equally important* is their poetic quality, an oral text that produces *aesthetic delight*.

We can support the idea that *these thinkers have not adequately recognized* this quality from the first three sentences of the passage, in which we learn that European thinkers generally regard names as being devoid of semantic content, and in which the author says that *other functions of names have been neglected*.

questions.prompt: The author most likely refers to Western Apache place names (last sentence of the third paragraph) in order to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipating Answer
explanationBlocks.body:
*Why* did the author bring up Western Apache place names? What was the bigger point being made in that immediate vicinity?

The author was stressing how rich in meaning the concise name of "beautifully ascended" is. Apparently Western Apache people named places with similarly beautifully concise names.

The author is conveying that the way Hopi named people and the way Western Apache named places are similar; both could be thought of as tiny poems that carry a lot of imagery.

choices.text: offer an example of how names can contain references not evident in their literal translations
choices.explanation:
"beautifully ascended" is an example of a name that contains references not evident in its literal translation. We have reason to believe that Western Apache place names would also have this quality, but the author doesn't provide such an example.

If this question stem had asked, "The author most likely refers to *Lomayayva* in order to", then this answer would apply.

choices.text: apply a commentator’s characterization of Western Apache place names to Hopi personal names
choices.explanation: The author is saying that Hopi personal names are "tiny imagist poems". They have the *same quality* that led a dude to call Western Apache place names "tiny imagist poems", so it would be fair to call Hope names "tiny imagist poems".

choices.text: contrast Western Apache naming practices with Hopi naming practices
choices.explanation: This isn't a moment of contrast; it's one of similarity. Both Western Apache place names and Hopi persona names are similar insofar as they both evoke a condensed image.

choices.text: demonstrate that other names besides Hopi names may have some semantic content
choices.explanation: The comparison does imply meaningful names beyond the Hopi example, but the local purpose is specifically to transfer the commentator's phrase tiny imagist poems to Hopi personal names. The word may is not an error merely because stronger evidence is available; B better captures what the comparison does.

choices.text: explain how a specific Hopi name refers subtly to a particular Western Apache site
choices.explanation: The passage compares condensed imagery; it does not say a Hopi name refers to an Apache location. Oraibi is the receiver's Hopi village, not a clan; the name giver belongs to Badger clan and the receiver to Lizard clan.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements describes an example of the function accorded to personal names under Lévi-Strauss's view?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body: In the 2nd sentence of the passage we learn that Strauss says that names are *primarily instruments of social classification*.

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipating Answer
explanationBlocks.body: We need to look for an answer that explains the social significance of a name; i.e., how does it reveal what class someone belongs to?

choices.text: Some parents select their children’s names from impersonal sources such as books.
choices.explanation: Books ≠ instruments of social classification

choices.text: Some parents wait to give a child a name in order to choose one that reflects the child’s looks or personality.
choices.explanation: Looks / personality ≠ instruments of social classification

choices.text: Some parents name their children in honor of friends or famous people.
choices.explanation:
Friends / famous people ≠ instruments of social classification

(if your friend was a famous/rich person, then maybe that would indirectly show that socially you're upper class, but that's too much of a stretch)

choices.text: Some family members have no parts of their names in common.
choices.explanation:
Unique names ≠ instruments of social classification

If we interpreted social classification as being, in part, a reflection of your extended family and its clout, or lack thereof, then we would expect family members to share parts of their names.

What's the point of being a Rockefeller or a Kennedy if you don't advertise that in your name? :)

choices.text: Some family names originated as identifications of their bearers’ occupations.
choices.explanation: A family name identifying an occupation places its bearer in a social category. That directly exemplifies social classification. The passage does not restrict classification to income or prestige, so no inference about the occupation's wealth is required.

questions.prompt: The primary function of the second paragraph is to

choices.text: present reasons why Hopi personal names can be treated as poetic compositions
choices.explanation: This is playing off the last sentence of the first paragraph, but the second paragraph didn't seem to offer any reasons we should call these names poetic compositions. That's what the third paragraph does.

choices.text: support the claim that Hopi personal names make reference to events in the recipient’s life
choices.explanation: The second paragraph does mention events in recipients' lives: birth, childhood initiation and puberty are naming occasions. But its main function is to show how names acquire meaningful references, including characteristics of the child and the name giver's clan. It is not chiefly evidence that the names refer to those life events.

choices.text: argue that the fact that Hopis receive many names throughout life refutes European theories about naming
choices.explanation: Receiving several names is described, not used by itself as a refutation. The meaningful references come from features such as the child's characteristics and the name giver's clan, which is explicitly different from the child's clan.

choices.text: illustrate ways in which Hopi personal names may have semantic content
choices.explanation: The example little rabbit combines a child's size with the totem animal of the name giver's clan. That directly illustrates semantic content: the name communicates something. The surrounding naming occasions and practices provide context. No reluctant best-available argument is needed.

choices.text: demonstrate that the literal translation of Hopi personal names often obscures their true meaning
choices.explanation: The limitations of literal translation are developed in the third paragraph, beginning with an event not apparent in the name's literal translation. The question asks about the second paragraph. We do not need to claim obscure always implies active concealment.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, with which one of the following statements about Mill's view would the author of the passage be most likely to agree?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body:
Our initial reaction to this question stem is probably that the author would say, "you wrong, Mill!"

After all, Mill's sense that proper names are meaningless marks with no semantic content is contradicted by the Hopi naming traditions that the author highlights.

But LSAT loves to test small areas where the author agrees with her opponent.

Mill said that a name is a meaningless mark "to distinguish them from one another", and later in the first paragraph, the author indicates that Hopi names "confer an identity upon them".

That seems to overlap a bit. So the answer might be,
"She disagrees with his view that names don't have meaning (semantic content)"
or
"She agrees with him that one function of names is to identify / distinguish people".

choices.text: Its characterization of the function of names is too narrow to be universally applicable.
choices.explanation:
"You wrong, Mill!" Since Mill denies that names have any important meaning, the example of the Hopi names would not fit his characterization, since they are chock full of meaning.

To say "your characterization is too narrow to be universally applicable" just means "there's at least one example where your characterization is wrong". And Mill's characterization of names as "meaningless marks" definitely does not apply to Hopi names.

choices.text: It would be correct if it recognized the use of names as instruments of social classification.
choices.explanation: This is what Levi-Strauss would say to Mill, not what our author would say.

choices.text: Its influence single-handedly led scholars to neglect how names are used outside Europe.
choices.explanation: The author doesn't say anything nearly this strong or accusatory. She just says that Mill and Levi-Strauss has been very influential.

choices.text: It is more accurate than Lévi-Strauss’s characterization of the purpose of names.
choices.explanation:
The author would agree with Levi-Strauss, that one function of names is social classification. And the author would agree with Mill that one function of names is distinguishing one person from another.

But she disagrees with both Mill and Levi-Strauss in their denial of semantic content, so she doesn't really pick who is *less wrong* / *more accurate*.

choices.text: It is less relevant than Lévi-Strauss’s characterization in understanding Hopi naming practices.
choices.explanation:
The author would agree with Levi-Strauss, that one function of names is social classification. And the author would agree with Mill that one function of names is distinguishing one person from another.

Hopi names do both of those things, so there's no reason for the author to think that one of these characterizations is more relevant than the other to Hopi naming practices.

She mainly thinks that both of these characterizations, in denying semantic content, are NOT applicable to Hopi naming practices.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that each of the following features of Hopi personal names contributes to their poetic quality EXCEPT:

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body:
The last line of the first paragraph says,
*the images used to evoke [the historical or ritual events referred to] suggest the names are poetic.*

The end of the 3rd paragraph says,
*The condensed image this name evokes ... makes them "tiny imagist poems"*

The 2nd sentence of the last paragraph says,
*the names can be understood as oral texts that produce aesthetic delight*

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
We'll look for four answers that seem connected to the poetic / semantic properties of Hopi names and pick whatever's left.

It wouldn't surprise me if the wrong answer used Mill's or Levi-Strauss's characterizations (distinguish people from each other / convey social classification)

choices.text: their ability to be understood as oral texts
choices.explanation: Second sentence of the last paragraph.

choices.text: their use of condensed imagery to evoke events
choices.explanation: Last sentence of the 3rd paragraph.

choices.text: their capacity to produce aesthetic delight
choices.explanation: Second sentence of the last paragraph.

choices.text: their ability to confer identity upon individuals
choices.explanation: This is Mill's characterization of names (second sentence of the 1st paragraph), and he certainly doesn't think names have a poetic (or any other semantic) quality.

choices.text: their ability to subtly convey meaning
choices.explanation:
This is more gist-y than expressed in verbatim, but the first sentence of the 3rd paragraph would probably qualify. Everything in the third paragraph leads into the final description of "tiny imagist poems".

The fact that there is more to the story than the literal translation is a quality we often associate with poetry (the literal translation might mean one thing, but the symbolism or contextual associations are part of the poetic meaning).

questions.prompt: The author's primary purpose in writing the passage is to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
In the first paragraph, we can see several potential Frameworks being at play:

*Challenge Position*
****position****: names don't have semantic content
****author****: yes they do, sometimes ... check out Hopi names

*Highlight Noteworthy*
****usual / mainstream****: names don't have semantic content / just signify who we are and betray some social class stuff / European thinkers and European names
****overlooked / important****: other societies, such as the Hopi, use names with other functions and meanings

*Illustrate General Claim*
****general claim****: some societies use names in non-European ways, with extra functions and meanings
****specific illustration****: the Hopi

choices.text: present an anthropological study of Hopi names
choices.explanation: This passage definitely presents a lot of information about Hopi names, but there's no anthropological study cited, and this answer would lose the broader context of contrasting how the Hopi use names with how other societies and European thinkers typically think about names.

choices.text: propose a new theory about the origin of name
choices.tag: Out of Scope: new theory / origin
choices.explanation: No one is discussing the origins of names. We're talking about the function of names. And the author isn't proposing a new theory. She's just highlighting some often overlooked examples of how names are used in non-European ways.

choices.text: describe several competing theories of names
choices.explanation: The author introduces two influential views, then argues that Hopi names show their limits. It is not a neutral description of competing theories. There is no need to define several as necessarily at least three.

choices.text: criticize two influential views of names
choices.explanation:
This reads a little harsh for me at first, even though I like the gist of "refuting the idea that Mill and Levi-Strauss (who are identified as influential views of names) have about names having no semantic content".

What makes me feel better about this as the overall purpose is that the author circles back in the final paragraph to make sure she lands a knockout blow: *this view of Hopi names is thus* *****opposed***** *not only to M's but also to LS's.*

And since the last sentence is normative / prescriptive (*what interpreters need to do is ...*), it's obliquely criticizing Mill and Levi-Strauss for having not done that.

choices.text: explain the cultural origins of names
choices.explanation:
The debate here is about the function of names, not their cultural origins. Also, the author isn't thinking that what is true of the Hopis is therefore "the cultural origin of names".

She explores the Hopi's naming conventions simply to show that the way names are defined by Mill and Levi-Strauss is too limiting to accommodate certain frequently overlooked societies.

passages.title: Homing Pigeons
passages.text:
Homing pigeons can be taken from their lofts and transported hundreds of kilometers in covered cages to unfamiliar sites and yet, when released, be able to choose fairly accurate homeward bearings within a minute and fly home. Aside from reading the minds of the experimenters (a possibility that has not escaped investigation), there are two basic explanations for the remarkable ability of pigeons to “home”: the birds might keep track of their outward displacement (the system of many short-range species such as honeybees); or they might have some sense, known as a “map sense,” that would permit them to construct an internal image of their environment and then “place” themselves with respect to home on some internalized coordinate system.

The first alternative seems unlikely. One possible model for such an inertial system might involve an internal magnetic compass to measure the directional leg of each journey. Birds transported to the release site wearing magnets or otherwise subjected to an artificial magnetic field, however, are only occasionally affected. Alternately, if pigeons measure their displacement by consciously keeping track of the direction and degree of acceleration and deceleration of the various turns, and timing the individual legs of the journey, simply transporting them in the dark, with constant rotations, or under complete anesthesia ought to impair or eliminate their ability to orient. These treatments, however, have no effect. Unfortunately, no one has yet performed the crucial experiment of transporting pigeons in total darkness, anesthetized, rotating, and with the magnetic field reversed all at the same time.

The other alternative, that pigeons have a “map sense,” seems more promising, yet the nature of this sense remains mysterious. Papi has posited that the map sense is olfactory: that birds come to associate odors borne on the wind with the direction in which the wind is blowing, and so slowly build up an olfactory map of their surroundings. When transported to the release site, then, they only have to sniff the air en route and/or at the site to know the direction of home. Papi conducted a series of experiments showing that pigeons whose nostrils have been plugged are poorly oriented at release and home slowly.

One problem with the hypothesis is that Schmidt-Koenig and Phillips failed to detect any ability in pigeons to distinguish natural air (presumably laden with olfactory map information) from pure, filtered air. Papi’s experimental results, moreover, admit of simpler, nonolfactory explanations. It seems likely that the behavior of nostril-plugged birds results from the distracting and traumatic nature of the experiment. When nasal tubes are used to bypass the olfactory chamber but allow for comfortable breathing, no disorientation is evident. Likewise, when the olfactory epithelium is sprayed with anesthetic to block smell-detection but not breathing, orientation is normal.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

How homing pigeons are able to navigate back home from unfamiliar distant locations.

**Framework**

Answer / Explain

**Main Point**

Scientists have investigated several explanations for pigeons' homing ability, including tracking their own displacement (like bees) and having a "map sense" (possibly olfactory), but no theory has been definitively proven. *Most Valuable Sentence: "The other alternative, that pigeons have a 'map sense,' seems more promising, yet the nature of this sense remains mysterious." (P3)*

**P1: Two Main Theories for Homing Ability**

Pigeons can navigate home over long distances, and researchers have proposed two main ideas to explain this: either pigeons track their journey step by step, or they have a kind of mental "map sense" that gives them their location relative to home.

**P2: Challenges to the Displacement/Tracking Theory**

Most attempts to disrupt route tracking have not prevented homing, although interfering with magnetic cues has occasionally succeeded. The crucial experiment combining the proposed disruptions has not been performed, so these results challenge displacement tracking without conclusively ruling it out.

**P3: Investigating the “Map Sense” Hypothesis**

A map sense looks more promising than displacement tracking, but the proposed olfactory version faces objections—one scientist, Papi, showed that plugging pigeons’ nostrils seems to impair their homing.

**P4: Problems with the Olfactory Theory**

There are issues with the smell-based map idea—other researchers couldn’t show that pigeons notice differences between scented and unscented air, and further experiments suggest that plugging nostrils may just be distracting or stressful for the birds, not actually related to their sense of smell.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: The ability of pigeons to locate and return to their homes from distant points is unlike that of any other species.
It is likely that some map sense accounts for the homing ability of pigeons, but the nature of that sense has not been satisfactorily identified.
The majority of experiments on the homing ability of pigeons have been marked by design flaws.
The mechanisms underlying the homing ability of pigeons can best be identified through a combination of laboratory research and field experimentation.
The homing ability of pigeons is most likely based on a system similar to that used by many short-range species.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which one of the following is ordinarily true regarding how homing pigeons "home"?

choices.text: Each time they are released at a specific site they fly home by the same route.
When they are released they take only a short time to orient themselves before selecting their route home.
Each time they are released at a specific site they take a shorter amount of time to orient themselves before flying home.
They travel fairly long distances in seemingly random patterns before finally deciding on a route home.
Upon release they travel briefly in the direction opposite to the one they eventually choose.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following experiments would best test the "possibility that has not escaped investigation" referred to in the second sentence of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The "possibility" referred to is that maybe homing pigeons are finding their way home by reading the minds of the experimenters.

i.e. The pigeons live at the Science Lab on Darwin Street. One day, the experimenters blindfold the pigeons or put them in a dark cage and then transport them to some place to release them and see if they can find their way home. When they release the pigeons, the pigeons are like, "Where the heck is home? Hold on, let me read this experimenter's mind ... Okay, that experimenter over there in the khakis is thinking something like '*I wonder if these pigeons will find their way back to Darwin Street.'* Hey, fellow pigeons! I have a clue: Darwin Street."

It's a pretty exotic hypothesis. How could we test whether they were reading the mind's of experimenters in order to get their directions home?

Maybe we could tell the experimenters the wrong location? Hire an Uber driver to drive the pigeons to the release point, but tell the Uber driver that these pigeons came from the Bird Lab on Big Bird Avenue. If the pigeons are really reading people's minds, then they'll hear the Uber driver thinking, '*I wonder if these pigeons will make it back to Big Bird Avenue'* and fly there, instead of back to the Science Lab on Darwin Street.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: It's hard to predict an answer here, but it should help us test whether pigeons are reading the thoughts of the people releasing them, in order to find out the directions home.

choices.text: an experiment in which the handlers who transported, released, and otherwise came into contact with homing pigeons released at an unfamiliar site were unaware of the location of the pigeons’ home
choices.explanation:
If the experimenters don't know where *home* is, then the pigeons won't be able to figure out where home is by reading the experimenters' minds.

So if they release the pigeons and the pigeons make it home anyway, then clearly the pigeons are not relying on reading the minds of experimenters'.

If they don't make it home when the experimenters are clueless (but used to make it home when the experimenters *did* know the location of the pigeons' home), then that would strongly suggest that the pigeons *were* reading their minds.

choices.text: an experiment in which the handlers who transported, released, and otherwise came into contact with homing pigeons released at an unfamiliar site were asked not to display any affection toward the pigeons
choices.explanation: It's not clear how experimenters showing vs. not showing affection would have anything to do with testing to see whether pigeons are reading their minds for directions.

choices.text: an experiment in which the handlers who transported, released, and otherwise came into contact with homing pigeons released at an unfamiliar site were asked not to speak to each other throughout the release process
choices.explanation:
It's not clear how experimenters being totally quiet vs. talking to each other would have anything to do with testing to see whether pigeons are reading their minds for directions.

The hypothesis isn't that pigeons are *listening* to hear the experimenters talk about directions. It's that the pigeons are *reading their minds*, which requires no spoken volume.

choices.text: an experiment in which all the homing pigeons released at an unfamiliar site had been raised and fed by individual researchers rather than by teams of handlers
choices.explanation: It's not clear how pigeons' being raised by an individual vs. by a team of handlers would have anything to do with testing to see whether pigeons can read the minds of humans in order to figure out directions home.

choices.text: an experiment in which all the homing pigeons released at an unfamiliar site were exposed to a wide variety of unfamiliar sights and sounds
choices.explanation:
It's not clear how exposing the pigeons to weird sights and sounds vs. not exposing them to that would have anything to do with testing to see whether pigeons are reading our minds in order to figure out the directions home.

Presumably, once our mildly abusive barrage of unfamiliar sights and sounds subside, a mind-reading pigeon would just be like, "Okaaaaay. *That* was weird. Well, anyway. Let's read these humans' minds for directions and head back home."

questions.prompt: Information in the passage supports which one of the following statements regarding the "first alternative" (first sentence of the second paragraph) for explaining the ability of pigeons to "home"?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body: The first alternative is tracking outward displacement. An internal magnetic compass is one proposed model, and consciously tracking turns and timing is another. Magnetic interventions occasionally affect orientation, while the darkness, rotation and anesthesia treatments described have no effect. The combined crucial experiment has not been performed. The evidence makes the explanation seem unlikely, not conclusively impossible. The passage discusses magnetic, not electric, fields.

choices.text: It has been conclusively ruled out by the results of numerous experiments.
choices.explanation:
The beginning of the 2nd paragraph said that this explanation "seems **unlikely**". That's not nearly as strong as "conclusively ruled out".

In fact, to somewhat contradict this, the author's final sentence of the 2nd paragraph is even suggesting that "we can't fully rule out this hypothesis until someone performs the crucial study of doing W, X, Y, and Z all at the same time."

choices.text: It seems unlikely because there are no theoretical models that could explain how pigeons track displacement.
choices.explanation:
The 2nd sentence of the 2nd paragraph says that there *is* a theoretical model that could explain it:

"one **possible model** for such an inertial system could be ..."

The author tells us that research has seemed to rule out this model as being the correct description of how pigeons track displacement, but ruling out a possible model is different from "there are no theoretical models that could explain it".

choices.text: It has not, to date, been supported by experimental data, but neither has it been definitively ruled out.
choices.explanation: The described studies do not establish a displacement-tracking mechanism, and the author calls it unlikely. The combined crucial experiment has not been performed, so it is not conclusively ruled out. Magnetic interventions occasionally affect birds, unlike the other treatments described; do not change occasionally into never. The conclusion rests on the whole experimental discussion, not on treating seems as a formal marker of uncertainty by itself.

choices.text: It seems unlikely in theory, but recent experimental results show that it may in fact be correct.
choices.explanation:
The first half of this matches up with the beginning of the 2nd paragraph, but the second half of this matches up with nothing.

All the experimental data in the 2nd paragraph went against the theory.

choices.text: It is not a useful theory because of the difficulty in designing experiments by which it might be tested.
choices.explanation:
Nothing in the 2nd paragraph suggests that the author thinks it's not a **useful** theory. The author just doesn't think it's accurate.

Also, the final sentence of the 2nd paragraph names a specific experiment by which researchers could test this theory, so saying that "it's difficulty to design experiments" seems somewhat contradicted.

questions.prompt: The author refers to "the system of many short-range species such as honeybees" (middle of the first paragraph) most probably in order to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
On Local Purpose questions (primarily to / serves to / in order to), the correct answer usually reinforces the idea that comes immediately before it.

In this case, the framing idea we hear before *honeybees* are mentioned is this:

*There are two basic explanations for the remarkable ability of pigeons to "home": the birds might keep track of their outward displacement (as honeybees do)*

So it seems like the author refers to the system of the honeybees as a way to add some plausibility to possible explanation #1.

Let's look for something like, "to show that other animal species find their way home by tracking their outward displacement".

choices.text: emphasize the universality of the ability to home
choices.explanation: The author is definitely never suggesting that all animals have the ability to home. In fact, this sentence calls the ability of pigeons to do so a "remarkable" ability.

choices.text: suggest that a particular explanation of pigeons’ homing ability is worthy of consideration
choices.explanation:
This is a good match for "to add some plausibility to possible explanation #1".

In an RC passage about kinglets (small birds), they're trying to figure out how they stay warm at night. The scientific community is hypothesizing that kinglets might huddle up together to conserve heat, and in the same breath we hear, "after all, that's what goldcrests do".

We can substantiate the plausibility of a potential explanation by showing a different situation where that explanation applies. In causal arguments in LR, we often refer to that form of strengthening answer choice as "More Cause, More Effect".

choices.text: discredit one of the less convincing theories regarding the homing ability of pigeons
choices.explanation:
The mention of *honeybees* is supposed to make ****more**** credible the theory that homing pigeons track their outward displacement.

Maybe some of us thought this answer was saying, "right ... it's supporting possible explanation 1, which means it's ****undermining**** possible explanation 2."

We can't think of it in zero-sum form like that. Supporting one explanation doesn't discredit an alternative explanation. Also it wouldn't make any sense to call explanation 2 (map sense) "one of the less convincing theories", especially given that the author ends up thinking this second explanation is more likely.

If people liked this answer because the author discredits explanation 1 at the outset of the 2nd paragraph (*The first alternative seems unlikely*), that would be the error of not dealing with the ****Local**** Purpose of mentioning honeybees. Even though the author eventually discredits explanation 1, telling us that honeybees use explanation 1 only has a supporting effect.

choices.text: criticize the techniques utilized by scientists investigating the nature of pigeons’ homing ability
choices.explanation: Nothing in this sentence is critical of anyone. It's just saying, very neutrally, that there are 2 possible explanations being considered for how pigeons home.

choices.text: illustrate why a proposed explanation of pigeons’ homing ability is correct
choices.explanation: The mention of honeybees is certainly trying to illustrate why a proposed explanation of pigeons' homing ability is *plausible*. But the author isn't picking a winner and saying, "Okay, it's decided then. If honeybees have the ability to home via tracking their outward displacement, then that's officially how pigeons do it too."

questions.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken Papi's theory regarding homing pigeons' homing ability?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
What *was* Papi's theory regarding pigeons' homing ability?

Papi thought that pigeons are able to find their way back home via an *olfactory map sense*. (Olfactory = sense of smell)

They learned which smells came from which direction, and thus had a smell map of their surroundings. So when they're released in an unfamiliar place, they can smell their way home.

So we're looking for something that would either
****provide an alternate explanation**** for how pigeons can find their way home,
or
